shared_core.title: Shared Core
shared_core.blurb: Cross-cutting foundations every track leans on. Cover these before specializing hard.

subjects.title: Math & Probability You Actually Use
subjects.why: You cannot debug loss, calibration, or sampling without this.
subjects.explainer:
Engineers who skip the math eventually hit a wall: a temperature knob that feels wrong, a KL term that blows up, a probability that is not a probability. You do not need a PhD. You need fluency with vectors and matrices as the language of embeddings and attention, gradients as the reason training moves, and entropy as the reason sampling explores.

Linear algebra shows up every time you multiply Q by K transpose. Probability shows up every time the model emits a next-token distribution. Information theory (cross-entropy, KL) is literally the training objective for modern LMs. Optimization (SGD, AdamW, schedules) decides whether your fine-tune converges or memorizes.

Common mistake: treating softmax temperature as a creativity dial without noticing it rescales the entire distribution and changes entropy. Another: confusing accuracy on a chat demo with calibrated probabilities the product needs for abstention.

In real systems this literacy lets you read a training curve, argue about whether top-p is hiding a bug, and talk to inference engineers about why speculative decoding acceptance rates tank when the draft model is miscalibrated.
subjects.project: Derive cross-entropy and KL by hand; simulate temperature/top-p and plot entropy vs temperature.

topics.title: Linear Algebra
topics.explainer: Almost everything in a model is a vector or a matrix. An embedding is a list of numbers; a layer is a matrix that maps one list to another. The dot product of two vectors measures how aligned they are, which is why it shows up as "similarity" in attention and in vector search. SVD tells you how much of a matrix is really needed: if a few singular values dominate, a low-rank version is nearly as good, and that is exactly the bet LoRA makes. Broadcasting is the habit of thinking in whole tensors with batch, sequence and hidden dimensions rather than loops. Learn to read shapes like [batch, seq, d_model] and most papers become much easier.

topics.title: Probability & Information
topics.explainer: A language model outputs a probability distribution over the next token. Training minimizes cross-entropy, the average surprise of the true token under the model, which is the same as maximum likelihood. KL divergence measures how far one distribution drifts from another; it is the leash in RLHF that keeps a tuned model near its reference. Entropy tells you how unsure the model is, which is useful for routing and abstention. Calibration asks whether "80% confident" is right 80% of the time, which is different from accuracy. Bayes is the mental tool for reasoning about evaluations: a 95%-accurate classifier on a 1% base-rate problem still produces mostly false alarms.

topics.title: Optimization
topics.explainer: Training is gradient descent: compute how the loss changes with each weight (backprop is the chain rule applied efficiently) and nudge weights the other way. Adam keeps running averages of gradients and their squares so each weight gets its own step size; AdamW separates weight decay from that update, which matters for generalization. Learning-rate warmup avoids blowing up early when statistics are noisy, then cosine or linear decay settles the model. Gradient clipping caps rare huge updates. Watch both training and validation loss: if validation rises while training falls you are overfitting; if both stay high you are underfitting or the learning rate is wrong.

quiz.q: Raising temperature generally…
choices: Increases entropy of the next-token distribution
quiz.why: Higher T flattens the distribution, raising entropy.

quiz.q: Cross-entropy LM training is closest to…
quiz.why: NLL/cross-entropy is MLE for next-token prediction.

quiz.q: LoRA works because weight updates during fine-tuning are often…
choices: Well approximated by a low-rank matrix
quiz.why: If a few singular values dominate the update, two thin matrices capture most of it.

quiz.q: A 95%-accurate detector on a 1%-prevalence problem will flag mostly…
quiz.why: Base rates dominate: about 5% of the 99% negatives get flagged, versus at most 1% true positives.

quiz.q: AdamW differs from Adam mainly by…
choices: Decoupling weight decay from the gradient update
quiz.why: Decoupled weight decay behaves more predictably and usually generalizes better.

subjects.title: Neural Nets & Representation Learning
subjects.why: Everything after this is a specialization of these ideas.
subjects.explainer:
A neural net is a stack of differentiable transforms that learn representations. Depth and width buy capacity; inductive biases buy sample efficiency. For LLMs the representation is a contextual embedding at every layer.

Residuals and norms (LayerNorm/RMSNorm) are why deep stacks train. Activations are not cosmetics. Regularization fights memorization — and in LLM fine-tunes, weight decay and LoRA rank interact in ways that surprise people who only know classical ML.

Common mistake: blaming the model when the learning rate is an order of magnitude off. Another: assuming more parameters always help when you are data-limited (see Chinchilla).

Representation thinking helps you decide when embeddings alone solve retrieval, when you need cross-encoders, and when a small specialist net beats prompting a giant LM.
subjects.project: Train a tiny MLP and a nano-scale LM; ablate width, depth, and learning rate.

topics.title: Building Blocks
topics.explainer: A neural network stacks simple layers: a linear map, a nonlinearity such as GELU or SiLU, and a loss at the end. Backprop sends error signals backward through every layer. Residual connections add the input of a block to its output, so gradients have a short path back and very deep networks stay trainable. Normalization (LayerNorm, RMSNorm) keeps activations in a sane range. Dropout and weight decay are regularizers that discourage memorization. Parameter counting is a practical skill: a transformer block has roughly 12·d² parameters (4·d² attention, 8·d² MLP), so you can sanity-check model sizes and memory before downloading anything.

topics.title: Representations & Scale
topics.explainer: Networks learn representations: internal coordinates where similar things sit close together. That is why pretrained models transfer, since the features learned on a huge corpus are reusable for your task with little extra data. Scaling laws describe how loss falls smoothly as you add parameters, data and compute, and Chinchilla showed that many early models were undertrained for their size (roughly 20 tokens per parameter is compute-optimal). Inductive bias is what an architecture assumes before seeing data: convolutions assume locality, attention assumes little. Large over-parameterized models can still generalize well, which overturned the classic "more parameters means more overfitting" intuition.

quiz.q: Chinchilla-style scaling emphasizes…
choices: Matching data size to model size for a compute budget
quiz.why: Compute-optimal training balances parameters and tokens.

quiz.q: A transformer block has roughly how many parameters per layer for hidden size d?
quiz.why: About 4·d² for attention projections and 8·d² for the MLP with 4x expansion.

quiz.q: Residual connections mainly help by…
choices: Giving gradients a short path through deep networks
quiz.why: The identity path keeps gradients flowing, so very deep stacks stay trainable.

subjects.title: LLM Mechanics
subjects.why: Shared vocabulary: tokens in, logits out, KV in between.
subjects.explainer:
Large language models are transformers trained to predict the next token. The operational stack is: tokenizer, embedding, blocks of attention plus MLP (or MoE), unembedding, softmax. Generation samples or argmaxes, appends the token, and repeats — unless constrained decode intervenes.

Tokenization is not free: fertility differs by language and code, which changes cost and latency. Attention is expensive; the KV cache avoids recomputing past keys/values each step. Positional schemes (RoPE) and attention variants (MHA, GQA, MQA, MLA) trade quality for memory.

Common mistake: comparing context windows without checking tokenizer and usable context after system prompt and tools. Another: swapping chat templates across families and wondering why quality collapsed.

This subject is the lingua franca across all five tracks.

resources.title: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al.)

subjects.project: Implement BPE (minbpe-style) and train a tiny GPT; inspect attention on a short prompt.

topics.title: Tokenization
topics.explainer: Models never see characters, only token ids. BPE and similar algorithms merge frequent byte pairs into a vocabulary of roughly 32k to 200k pieces. Fertility, the number of tokens per word, varies a lot by language and domain: code, Thai, or chemical names can cost several times more tokens than English prose, which hits both cost and context budget. Chat templates wrap messages with special tokens that mark roles; using the wrong template quietly degrades quality. Detokenization can split multi-byte characters across tokens, so streaming clients must buffer bytes. Always count tokens with the model's own tokenizer before you send.

topics.title: Attention & Blocks

subtopics.title: Causal mask and KV cache role

topics.explainer: A transformer block is attention followed by a feed-forward network, each wrapped in a residual connection and normalization. Attention lets every token gather information from earlier tokens, weighted by query-key similarity. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel. GQA and MQA share key/value heads across query heads to shrink the KV cache; MLA compresses keys and values into a smaller latent. RoPE encodes position by rotating query and key vectors so relative distance shows up in their dot product. The causal mask stops tokens from peeking at the future, which is exactly what makes caching earlier keys and values valid during generation.

topics.title: Generation
topics.explainer: Generation is a loop: run the model, get logits for the next token, pick one, append it, repeat. Greedy picks the top token; temperature reshapes the distribution (lower is sharper); top-k and top-p cut off the unlikely tail before sampling. Stop sequences end the loop. Constrained decoding masks tokens that would break a grammar or JSON schema, so output is valid by construction. Logprobs expose the model's confidence per token and are handy for classification and routing. Streaming sends tokens as they appear, which improves perceived latency but means your client must handle partial output and cancellation.

quiz.q: KV cache primarily avoids…
choices: Recomputing attention over past tokens each decode step
quiz.why: Cached K/V skip full prefill every decode step.

quiz.q: Lower temperature makes sampling…
quiz.why: Dividing logits by a smaller temperature sharpens the distribution toward the top token.

quiz.q: Why can text cost more tokens in Thai or code than in English prose?
quiz.why: Vocabularies trained mostly on English split other text into more pieces per word.

subjects.title: Long Context, Multimodal & MoE Basics
subjects.why: Modern models are not just short-text left-to-right stacks.
subjects.explainer:
Three extensions show up in every 2026 stack. Long context (100K to 1M+ tokens) changes retrieval versus stuffing tradeoffs, but attention cost and lost-in-the-middle still bite. Multimodal VLMs add vision (and sometimes audio) encoders; failure modes include OCR errors, layout blindness, and unsafe image instructions. Mixture-of-Experts activates a subset of experts per token — great for capacity per dollar, painful for serving (expert parallelism, load imbalance).

Common mistake: treating a 1M context model as a free database. Another: sending every PDF to a VLM when a parser plus text model is cheaper and more reliable.

Architects need these options in the build/buy matrix; inference engineers feel MoE on the interconnect; app engineers feel long context on the invoice.

resources.title: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al.)

subjects.project: Benchmark the same QA with short RAG versus long-context stuffing; compare cost, latency, accuracy.

topics.title: Long Context
topics.explainer: A model may accept 1M tokens, but usable context is smaller: recall of facts buried in the middle often drops ("lost in the middle"), and cost and latency grow with length. KV cache memory grows linearly with tokens, and attention compute grows quadratically during prefill, so long prompts are expensive to serve. Sparse, sliding-window and chunked attention variants trade some quality for efficiency. RoPE scaling methods stretch positional encodings beyond training length. RAG still wins when the corpus is bigger than any window, changes often, or needs access control per document. Measure with needle-in-a-haystack and, better, task-level evals on your own long documents.

topics.title: Multimodal & Speech
topics.explainer: Vision-language models usually bolt a vision encoder onto an LLM: the image is cut into patches, encoded, projected into the token embedding space, and treated like extra tokens. A single high-resolution image can cost hundreds to thousands of tokens. For documents, classic OCR or PDF text extraction is often cheaper and more accurate than sending page images, with the VLM as a fallback for charts and layout. Speech systems pair speech-to-text and text-to-speech with an LLM, or use native audio models for lower latency. New modalities bring new attack surfaces, such as instructions hidden in images or audio.

topics.title: Mixture of Experts
topics.explainer: Mixture-of-experts replaces the single feed-forward block with many experts and a small router that sends each token to the top-k of them (often 2 of 8, or 8 of 256). Only a fraction of the parameters run per token, so you get the quality of a big model at the compute of a smaller one. The catch is memory: all experts must be resident, so a 600B-parameter MoE still needs the HBM of a 600B model. Training adds load-balancing losses so experts are used evenly. Serving uses expert parallelism, which turns routing into all-to-all network traffic and makes batch composition matter.

quiz.q: MoE models typically…
choices: Activate a subset of experts per token
quiz.why: Sparsity is the point of MoE.

quiz.q: A 600B-parameter MoE that activates 37B per token still needs memory for…
quiz.why: All experts must be resident because any token may route to any expert.

quiz.q: RAG still beats a huge context window when…
choices: The corpus is small and static
The corpus is larger than the window or needs per-document access control
quiz.why: Windows have limits, cost scales with length, and ACLs are easier at retrieval time.

subjects.title: Evaluation Literacy
subjects.why: If you cannot measure it, you cannot improve or sell it.
subjects.explainer:
Evals turn probabilistic systems into engineering. Separate capability, safety, and cost. Offline golden sets catch regressions; online metrics catch drift. LLM-as-judge is useful and biased — calibrate it. Contamination silently inflates leaderboards.

Process metrics (right tool called?) matter as much as outcomes for agents. For RAG, measure retrieval and generation separately or you will fine-tune the wrong stage.

Common mistake: weeks of demos before twenty labeled cases. Another: tuning a judge until it agrees with you.

Ship a thin eval harness on day one; thicken it as the product hardens.
subjects.project: Build a 50-item golden set; score exact match plus LLM-judge; measure judge agreement.

topics.title: What to Measure
topics.explainer: Decide what "good" means before measuring. Capability (does it solve the task), safety (does it avoid harm and leaks), and cost/latency are separate axes and often trade off. For agents, outcome metrics (task done) and process metrics (steps, tool errors, policy violations) both matter. Offline evals on fixed sets catch regressions; online signals such as user edits, thumbs, and escalations catch what your set missed. Contamination happens when test items leaked into training data, inflating scores. Calibration and abstention matter in high-stakes domains: a model that says "I don't know" correctly is often worth more than one that is slightly more accurate.

topics.title: How to Run
topics.explainer: Start with a golden set: 50 to 200 real, labeled examples with clear rubrics, built before you tune anything. LLM-as-judge scales grading but has biases (position, verbosity, self-preference), so calibrate it against human labels and keep the judge model and prompt versioned. Put evals in CI so prompt or model changes fail the build when quality drops. Shadow traffic and A/B tests validate changes on real users safely. Keep an error taxonomy (retrieval miss, hallucination, format error, refusal) so failures turn into specific fixes rather than vague "the model is worse" complaints.

quiz.q: Best time to create a golden set is…
choices: With the first prompt, before the demo hardens
quiz.why: Early evals prevent demo-driven dead ends.

quiz.q: LLM-as-judge should be…
choices: Calibrated against human labels and versioned
quiz.why: Judges have position, verbosity and self-preference biases that drift with versions.

quiz.q: Contamination means…
choices: The eval set leaked into training data
quiz.why: Leaked test items inflate scores without real capability.

subjects.title: AI Security & Trust Basics
subjects.why: Tools turn models into attack surfaces.
subjects.explainer:
Prompt injection (direct and indirect), data/model poisoning, supply-chain risk (weights, MCP servers, plugins), and secret leakage through logs are everyday threats. OWASP LLM Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS give shared language; NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act shape enterprise buying.

Controls: least-privilege tools, sandboxes, egress allowlists, output validation, human approval for irreversible actions, and provenance for models and data.

Common mistake: a regex on user input while tools still hold broad SaaS tokens. Another: logging full prompts with PII into a third-party tracer.

Every track inherits this threat model.
subjects.project: Red-team a toy RAG+tools bot for indirect injection; document findings and mitigations.

topics.title: Threats
topics.explainer: LLM systems mix instructions and data in one channel, so prompt injection is the signature threat: direct when a user types it, indirect when it hides in a web page, email, PDF or tool result the model reads. Poisoning plants bad behavior in training or retrieval data. The supply chain now includes model weights, tokenizers, plugins and MCP servers, any of which can be malicious. Secrets pasted into prompts end up in logs and traces. Attackers can also query a model to extract its behavior or test whether a record was in its training data. Treat every model output as untrusted input to the next system.

topics.title: Controls
topics.explainer: You cannot reliably filter prompt injection, so design so it cannot do much damage. Give tools least privilege: narrow scopes, read before write, per-user credentials rather than a shared admin key. Run code and browsers in sandboxes with egress allowlists. Validate model output against schemas and business rules before acting on it. Put human approval in front of irreversible actions like sending money or email. Keep tamper-evident audit logs of prompts, tool calls and approvals so you can reconstruct incidents. Record provenance for models and data so you know exactly what was running when something went wrong.

quiz.q: Indirect prompt injection often arrives via…
quiz.why: Untrusted retrieved content is a classic channel.

quiz.q: The most reliable defense against prompt injection consequences is…
choices: Limiting what the model's tools can do
Asking the model to be careful
quiz.why: You cannot filter injection perfectly, so least privilege limits the damage.

quiz.q: Pickle-based model files are risky because…
choices: Loading them can execute arbitrary code
quiz.why: Pickle deserialization runs code; prefer safetensors.

tracks.name: AI Architect
tracks.role: Owns system shape: requirements to reference architecture, build/buy, governance, cost and risk. Day to day: ADRs, vendor bake-offs, security reviews, capacity models. Differs from AI Engineer (ships the app) and Infra (runs GPUs): you decide what gets built and why it survives a year.

subjects.title: Systems Thinking for AI Products
subjects.why: AI is a probabilistic subsystem; architecture must absorb that.
subjects.explainer:
Classical architecture assumes deterministic services. AI features return distributions, burn tokens, and fail semantically even when HTTP is 200. Your job is to place bounds: SLOs for latency and quality, human-in-the-loop where irreversible actions live, and clear ownership of model versus product metrics.

Decompose around bounded contexts, not around the newest framework. Prefer sync paths for user-facing chat and async workers for long agents. Design degraded modes (smaller model, cached answers, keyword search) the same way you design for AZ loss.

Common mistake: a single mega-agent diagram with no failure domains. Another: copying a Big Tech reference architecture that assumes their data platform.

Write ADRs that record the probabilistic assumptions — future you will need them when the model changes.
subjects.project: Write an ADR for customer-support AI: workflow vs agent, retrieval vs fine-tune, rollback plan.

topics.title: Requirements
topics.explainer: AI requirements need numbers on more axes than usual. Besides features, pin down latency (time to first token and total), quality (task success on an eval set), cost per request or per user per month, and availability. Ask where data may be processed and stored, and whether tenants must be isolated. Decide where humans review or approve. Write abuse cases alongside use cases: what happens when someone tries to jailbreak it, scrape it, or run up the bill? Requirements that skip these show up later as surprise invoices, compliance blockers, or a security incident.

topics.title: Decomposition
topics.explainer: Break the system along boundaries that fail and scale differently. Keep the synchronous user path thin and push slow work (enrichment, indexing, long agent runs) to async queues. Separate failure domains so a model provider outage degrades one feature instead of the whole product. Use strangler patterns to replace legacy flows incrementally rather than in a big bang. Design degraded modes up front: cached answers, a smaller fallback model, or a "we're busy, here's a form" path. A good decomposition makes it obvious which team owns which latency and cost budget.

quiz.q: A 200 OK from an LLM API guarantees…
quiz.why: Transport success is not task success.

quiz.q: Which is a non-functional requirement for an AI feature?
choices: p95 time to first token under 1 second
quiz.why: Latency targets constrain how, not what, the system does.

quiz.q: A degraded mode for an LLM feature could be…
choices: Serving a cached answer or a smaller fallback model
quiz.why: Planned degradation keeps users served when the main path fails.

subjects.title: ML / LLM System Lifecycle
subjects.why: Know data to production so you do not design dead ends.
subjects.explainer:
Hidden Technical Debt in ML Systems still applies — only now prompts, tools, and indexes are also config. Map data, train or adapt, eval, serve, monitor, feedback. Offline versus online features matter for classical ML; for LLMs the analogs are frozen corpora versus live retrieval and tool results.

Drift is not only statistical: prompt drift, schema drift, and harness drift break agents. Shadow and canary deployments need quality gates, not only error-rate gates.

Common mistake: treating the prompt store as tribal knowledge in Slack. Another: no owner for evaluation when the model vendor ships a silent upgrade.

Architects insist on lineage: which prompt, which index build, which model revision produced this answer.
subjects.project: Map a past project onto the lifecycle; list every place drift can hide.

topics.title: Pipeline

subtopics.title: Data to adapt to eval to serve to monitor

topics.explainer: An AI system is a pipeline, not a model: data flows into adaptation (prompts, RAG indexes, fine-tunes), into evaluation, into serving, and into monitoring that feeds back into data. Offline signals (eval scores) and online signals (user behavior) must both exist. Release with shadow, canary or blue-green deployments, exactly as with code. Track lineage so every response can be traced to a prompt version, model version, index snapshot and config. Without lineage you cannot answer the most common incident question: what changed?

topics.title: Debt and Drift
topics.explainer: AI systems accumulate unusual debt. Data drift shifts inputs; concept drift changes what the right answer is. Prompts and configs drift as people tweak them in production without review. Harness drift happens when the agent framework changes behavior underneath you. Glue code between models, retrievers and tools grows into a jungle with no tests. The fix is boring discipline: version prompts and configs like code, monitor input distributions, assign an owner to every metric, and schedule regular eval refreshes so the golden set still reflects real traffic.

quiz.q: Prompt changes should be…
quiz.why: Prompts are production config.

quiz.q: Lineage lets you answer…
choices: What prompt, model, index and config produced this response
quiz.why: Lineage links outputs to every versioned input.

quiz.q: Concept drift means…
choices: The correct answer for the same input changes over time
quiz.why: For example, policy or price changes make old answers wrong.

subjects.title: Model Landscape Literacy for Architects
subjects.why: You cannot choose platforms without knowing model shapes.
subjects.explainer:
Frontier APIs, open-weight dense models, MoE, small on-device models, and VLMs are different animals for cost, control, and failure modes. Licensing (open weights versus open source versus proprietary API) constrains commercialization. Context length, tool-calling quality, and multilingual fertility change the architecture more than brand names.

Common mistake: picking a model from a leaderboard without matching the client's data residency and latency envelope. Another: ignoring tokenizer and chat-template lock-in when planning multi-vendor routing.

Keep a living scorecard: capability, controllability, cost, compliance, community.
subjects.project: Build a one-page scorecard comparing one frontier API, one open 70B, and one small edge model for a fixed use case.

topics.title: Model Types
topics.explainer: Know the categories. Frontier APIs give top capability with no ops burden but less control over data, versions and cost. Open-weight dense models can be self-hosted and tuned, at the cost of running GPUs. MoE models give big-model quality with smaller compute per token but large memory footprints. Small language models run cheaply on CPUs, phones and edge boxes for narrow tasks. Vision-language and speech models add modalities with their own latency and cost profiles. Most real architectures mix several of these behind one gateway.

topics.title: Selection
topics.explainer: Leaderboards are a starting filter, not an answer: benchmarks leak into training data and rarely match your domain. Read licenses carefully, since "open weights" may still restrict commercial use or user counts. Tokenizer and chat template choices create quiet lock-in in prompts and fine-tunes. Check tool-calling and structured output maturity if you are building agents. The only reliable selection method is running two or three candidates on your own golden set and comparing quality, latency and cost per successful task.

quiz.q: Open weights always means…
choices: Not automatically OSI open source or unlimited commercial rights
quiz.why: Weights, license, and API product are distinct.

quiz.q: The most reliable way to choose a model for a client is…
choices: Running candidates on the client's own golden set
quiz.why: Your data and tasks decide; benchmarks are only a filter.

quiz.q: Small language models are a good fit for…
quiz.why: They trade breadth for cost, latency and privacy.

subjects.title: Reference Architectures
subjects.why: Reuse proven shapes; do not invent a snowflake per client.
subjects.explainer:
Most enterprise AI systems are compositions of a few patterns: request/response LLM API, RAG with citations, batch enrichment, event-driven agent workers, and human review queues. Layer edge, API, orchestration, model gateway, and data carefully. Separate control plane (prompts, policies, evals) from data plane (tokens, embeddings, tool I/O).

Multi-region and multi-tenant designs need sticky considerations for prefix caches and per-tenant keys.

Common mistake: drawing microservices everywhere when a modular monolith with a model gateway would ship sooner. Another: no shared observability layer, so every squad invents tracing.

Your deliverable is a one-pager engineers can build from — not a slide museum.
subjects.project: Produce a one-page reference for multi-tenant RAG SaaS with auth, quotas, and audit.

topics.title: Patterns
topics.explainer: A handful of patterns cover most AI products. An LLM API facade wraps providers behind your own interface. RAG with citations grounds answers in your documents. Batch enrichment runs models over large datasets offline for classification or extraction. Agent workers execute multi-step tasks from a queue with tools and budgets. Human review queues route low-confidence or high-risk outputs to people. Knowing these lets you sketch a credible architecture in a first client meeting and then adjust for their constraints.

topics.title: Layering
topics.explainer: Draw AI systems in layers: edge (auth, rate limits), API, orchestration (prompts, agents, workflows), model (gateway, serving), and data (indexes, stores). Separate the control plane, where policies, routing rules, prompt versions and budgets live, from the data plane that handles requests. Plan multi-region failover for both models and indexes. Shared services such as identity, billing, observability and secrets should be reused, not rebuilt per feature. Clear layers make it easy to swap a model or vendor without rewriting the product.

quiz.q: Control plane for AI usually includes…
choices: Prompt registry, policies, evals, routing config
quiz.why: Control plane governs how models are used.

quiz.q: Separating control plane from data plane means…
choices: Policies and configs are managed apart from request handling
quiz.why: Policy changes then do not require redeploying request paths.

quiz.q: Which pattern best fits classifying 10 million records overnight?
quiz.why: Batch APIs and offline pipelines are cheaper and simpler for bulk work.

subjects.title: Build vs Buy vs Host
subjects.why: Wrong call here burns months of runway.
subjects.explainer:
Decision dimensions: capability ceiling, latency and region, data control and sovereignty, unit economics, lock-in and exit. Options: frontier APIs, cloud managed (Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, Vertex), open-weight self-host, and hybrid routing (cheap model with escalation).

Gateways like LiteLLM or custom routers buy portability but add an ops surface. Self-hosting shifts spend from tokens to GPUs, people, and reliability engineering.

Common mistake: self-hosting for 'savings' at low volume where APIs would be cheaper. Another: all-in on one vendor with no export path for prompts, evals, and traces.

Score options with explicit weights tied to the client's constraints — not your favorite stack.
subjects.project: Scored decision matrix: Bedrock vs Azure AI Foundry vs self-hosted vLLM for a mid-market client.

topics.title: Dimensions
topics.explainer: Compare options on five axes. Capability ceiling: can anything but a frontier model do the task? Latency and region: where must inference run? Sovereignty: can data or weights leave the boundary? Unit economics: what is the cost per successful task at expected volume? Lock-in and exit: how hard is it to switch providers? Score each option against these explicitly with the client so the decision survives a change of leadership or a price change.

topics.title: Options
topics.explainer: The realistic menu is: frontier APIs, cloud-managed platforms (Bedrock, Vertex, Azure AI Foundry), self-hosted open weights on your GPUs, or a hybrid with routing. Hybrid is common: cheap or private traffic goes to a self-hosted model, hard queries go to a frontier API. A gateway layer (LiteLLM, Envoy AI Gateway, Kong, or a cloud gateway) gives one API, keys, budgets and fallbacks across all of them. Self-hosting only pays off above a utilization threshold, so do the math first.

quiz.q: Hybrid routing primarily optimizes…
choices: Cost/quality by sending easy work to cheaper models
quiz.why: Route by difficulty/risk to control spend.

quiz.q: Self-hosting open weights usually pays off when…
choices: You need the best frontier model
quiz.why: GPU cost is fixed per hour; high utilization drives down cost per token.

quiz.q: A gateway layer gives you…
choices: One API, central keys, budgets and fallbacks across providers
quiz.why: It decouples apps from providers.

subjects.title: Enterprise Data Platforms for AI
subjects.why: Most AI projects fail on data access, quality, and rights.
subjects.explainer:
Lakehouse/warehouse, vector and keyword indexes, catalogs, lineage, and quality monitors are the substrate. Rights (training versus inference use), PII/PHI, and freshness SLAs constrain design. Chunking and metadata standards are architectural decisions, not afterthoughts.

Common mistake: a pilot on a CSV export that cannot be refreshed in production. Another: embeddings of secrets that now live forever in a vector store.

Define data contracts for each retrieval slice before model selection.
subjects.project: Design a data contract and retrieval slice for one domain including PII handling.

topics.title: Platform
topics.explainer: AI rides on the data platform. A lakehouse or warehouse holds governed source data. Retrieval needs both vector and keyword indexes, ideally fed from the same pipeline. A catalog with lineage and quality checks tells you where each chunk came from and whether it is fresh. Embedding stores must be versioned with the embedding model, because changing models means re-embedding everything. Think about access patterns early: per-user ACL filtering at query time is far easier if permissions are stored as chunk metadata from day one.

topics.title: Rights and Quality
topics.explainer: Before data feeds a model, know whether you have the right to use it for that purpose, especially for training. Scan for PII, PHI and secrets before indexing. Set freshness SLAs so stale documents do not produce confident wrong answers. Standardize chunking and metadata (source, owner, ACL, timestamp) across teams. Plan deletion end to end: removing a source document must also remove its chunks, embeddings, cache entries and any derived summaries, or you will fail a right-to-erasure request.

quiz.q: Deleting a source document requires…
choices: Also deleting or regenerating derived embeddings/chunks
quiz.why: Derived indexes retain content unless purged.

quiz.q: Switching embedding models requires…
quiz.why: Vectors from different models are not comparable.

quiz.q: Per-user permission filtering in RAG is easiest when…
choices: ACLs are stored as chunk metadata
quiz.why: Filter at retrieval time using metadata, not in the prompt.

subjects.title: Model Gateways, Semantic Cache & Routing
subjects.why: The gateway is where cost, policy, and portability meet.
subjects.explainer:
A model gateway centralizes auth, budgets, routing, fallbacks, and observability across providers. Semantic caching (embedding-similar prompt reuse) can slash cost for FAQs but risks stale or cross-tenant leaks if keyed poorly. Structured rate limits and circuit breakers protect both wallet and upstream SLAs.

Common mistake: caching on raw prompt strings only, missing near-duplicates — or worse, caching across tenants. Another: a gateway that rewrites prompts silently and breaks eval baselines.

Treat the gateway as a product with its own SLOs and audit log.
subjects.project: Sketch a gateway: routes, cache key design, tenant isolation, and fallback chain.

topics.title: Gateway Features
topics.explainer: A model gateway sits between apps and model providers. It normalizes APIs so apps call one interface, holds provider keys so apps never see them, and enforces per-team budgets and rate limits. It adds fallbacks (switch provider on errors) and hedging (send a second request if the first is slow). Policy hooks run PII redaction, prompt-injection screening or content filters on the way in and out. Every call emits a unified trace with tokens, cost and latency, which makes it the natural place to measure and govern AI usage.

topics.title: Semantic Cache
topics.explainer: A semantic cache returns a stored answer when a new prompt is close enough in embedding space to an old one. It can cut cost and latency sharply for FAQ-like traffic. The risks are wrong hits and leaks: the similarity threshold must be tuned on real pairs, keys must include tenant, model and prompt version, and TTLs must respect how fast the truth changes. Never share cache entries across tenants or permission levels. Provide bypass rules for personalized, time-sensitive or tool-using requests.

quiz.q: Semantic cache keys should…
choices: Include tenant and policy scope, not only text similarity
Be a global hash of the prompt alone
quiz.why: Isolation and policy beat naive similarity.

quiz.q: Hedging in a gateway means…
choices: Sending a backup request if the first is slow
quiz.why: Hedging trades some extra cost for lower tail latency.

quiz.q: Semantic cache entries must never be shared across…
quiz.why: Cross-tenant hits leak data.

subjects.title: Security Architecture & Threat Modeling
subjects.why: Own the threat model before engineers write the loop.
subjects.explainer:
Assets include models, data, tools, and keys. Attack paths include indirect injection via retrieval, confused-deputy tool abuse, and supply-chain tampering of MCP servers. Map STRIDE-like analysis onto LLM apps; align with OWASP LLM Top 10 and ATLAS techniques.

Architectural controls: network isolation, sandboxes, tool allowlists, approval gates, vaulted secrets, immutable audits.

Common mistake: bolting a content filter on outputs while tools can still wire money. Another: shared service accounts for all agents.

Threat models are living documents — update when tools expand.
subjects.project: STRIDE-style threat model for an agent with email-read and ticket-write tools.

topics.title: Threat Modeling
topics.explainer: Start by listing assets: model weights, system prompts, training and retrieval data, tool credentials, user data. Then trace how untrusted text reaches the model, including indirect paths through documents, web pages, emails and tool outputs. The confused deputy is the key agent risk: the agent has permissions the attacker lacks and can be talked into using them. Add supply chain (models, packages, MCP servers) and abuse at scale (scraping, cost attacks). STRIDE still works; extend it with MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP LLM Top 10.

topics.title: Controls
topics.explainer: Controls that work regardless of model behavior: put tools and code execution in network-isolated sandboxes; use allowlists and human approvals for sensitive actions; keep secrets in a vault and inject short-lived, scoped tokens per call; log every prompt, tool call and approval in immutable storage; and schedule red-team exercises on a cadence, not once. Prefer architectural limits (the agent literally cannot reach the payments API) over prompt instructions (please don't touch payments).

quiz.q: A confused deputy in agent systems is often…
choices: A powerful tool identity abused via malicious instructions
quiz.why: Over-privileged tools act on injected instructions.

quiz.q: Which control is architectural rather than prompt-based?
choices: "Never reveal secrets" in the system prompt
Network policy that blocks the agent from the payments API
quiz.why: Architectural limits hold even when the model is tricked.

quiz.q: Which framework catalogs adversarial tactics against ML systems?
quiz.why: ATLAS extends ATT&CK-style tactics to AI systems.

subjects.title: Governance, Risk & Compliance
subjects.why: Enterprise deals die on GRC, not demos.
subjects.explainer:
EU AI Act risk tiers, NIST AI RMF functions, ISO 42001 AIMS, and sector rules (HIPAA, SOC2, FedRAMP) define the operating theater. Model cards, system cards, DPIAs, and human oversight roles are deliverables, not paperwork theater.

Common mistake: claiming 'we use OpenAI so we are compliant.' Another: no incident response playbook for model hallucinations that caused customer harm.

Architects translate legal tiers into technical controls and evidence packs.
subjects.project: Classify a proposed system under EU AI Act tiers; draft a conformity checklist.

topics.title: Frameworks
topics.explainer: The EU AI Act sorts systems into risk tiers, with heavy obligations for high-risk uses and transparency duties for general-purpose models. NIST AI RMF gives a voluntary govern-map-measure-manage structure widely used in the US. ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable AI management system standard, similar in spirit to ISO 27001. Sector rules (HIPAA, financial model risk guidance such as SR 11-7, and others) still apply. Contracts flow obligations down to vendors, so your model provider's terms become part of your compliance story.

topics.title: Operating Model
topics.explainer: Governance becomes real through artifacts and roles. Model and system cards document purpose, data, evals and limitations. AI impact assessments (often alongside DPIAs) record risks and mitigations before launch. Name who provides human oversight and what they can override. Extend incident response to cover AI failures such as harmful outputs, data leaks, or agent misbehavior. Keep evidence (eval results, approvals, change logs) organized so an auditor can follow it without a week of archaeology.

quiz.q: ISO 42001 is best described as…
quiz.why: 42001 is AIMS — management system for AI.

quiz.q: The EU AI Act primarily classifies systems by…
choices: Risk tier of the use case
quiz.why: Obligations scale with risk of the application.

quiz.q: NIST AI RMF's four functions are…
quiz.why: These structure AI risk work across the lifecycle.

subjects.title: Cost Modeling & AI FinOps
subjects.why: Unit economics decide whether the architecture is viable.
subjects.explainer:
Model cost as dollars per million tokens in and out, cache hit savings, tool-call overhead, and GPU-hour TCO for self-host. Add egress, storage for indexes, and eval spend. Quotas, routing tiers, and batch versus realtime are architectural levers.

Common mistake: ignoring output tokens (often more expensive) or tool loops that multiply calls. Another: no chargeback, so every team treats the LLM budget as infinite.

Build a spreadsheet the CFO can read and the engineer can update.
subjects.project: Spreadsheet: tokens in/out, cache hit rate, tool calls, GPU-hour alternative; find break-even.

topics.title: Unit Economics
topics.explainer: Learn to compute cost per request: input tokens times input price plus output tokens times output price, with output typically 3 to 5 times more expensive. Prompt or prefix caching discounts repeated input heavily. For self-hosting, convert GPU-hour cost and measured throughput into dollars per million tokens. Do not forget egress, storage for logs and indexes, eval runs, and human review time, which can exceed model spend. The useful metric is cost per successful task, not cost per call.

topics.title: Controls
topics.explainer: Cost control is mostly architecture. Set per-tenant and per-feature budgets enforced at the gateway. Route easy queries to small models and escalate only when needed. Move anything that is not interactive to batch APIs, often half price. Show teams their spend (showback) or charge it back so incentives line up. Alert on anomalies such as a sudden jump in tokens per request, which usually means a prompt bug, a loop, or abuse.

quiz.q: Prefix caching helps most when…
choices: Many requests share a long stable prompt prefix
quiz.why: Shared prefixes make KV reuse pay off.

quiz.q: 1,000 input tokens at $3/M plus 500 output tokens at $15/M costs…
The best unit metric for AI cost is usually…
quiz.why: Failed or retried tasks hide in per-call numbers.

subjects.title: Privacy, PII & Data Minimization
subjects.why: Privacy failures end deals and careers.
subjects.explainer:
Minimize what enters prompts and logs. Redact PII before tracing vendors. Prefer retrieval filters and field-level encryption over stuffing whole records. Understand training-use opt-outs on APIs versus self-host. Retention and right-to-be-forgotten must include vector indexes.

Common mistake: pasting production rows into a consumer ChatGPT account during debugging. Another: indefinite retention of session transcripts 'for quality.'

Privacy is an architecture constraint equal to latency.
subjects.project: Design a PII redaction path for prompts, tools, logs, and embeddings with deletion workflow.

topics.title: Minimization
topics.explainer: The cheapest data to protect is data you never send. Strip or mask identifiers before prompts leave your boundary. Redact logs and traces by default. Apply field-level controls so the model sees only fields needed for the task. Review vendor data processing agreements for retention, training use and subprocessors, and turn off training-on-your-data where offered. Minimization reduces breach impact, regulatory scope and vendor risk all at once.

topics.title: Operations
topics.explainer: Privacy is an ongoing operation. Set retention schedules for prompts, outputs and traces. When a user or document is deleted, purge it from indexes, caches and memories too. Review who can read raw logs and traces. Have a breach playbook that covers AI-specific leaks such as a model repeating another user's data. Respect data residency by pinning processing regions, including for embeddings and evals, not just the main model call.

quiz.q: Right-to-be-forgotten for RAG requires…
choices: Purging derived chunks/embeddings, not only the source row
quiz.why: Derived artifacts retain personal data.

quiz.q: Data minimization reduces…
choices: Breach impact, regulatory scope and vendor risk
quiz.why: Data never sent cannot leak.

quiz.q: Residency compliance must include…
choices: Embeddings, logs and evals as well
quiz.why: Any processing step can move data out of region.

subjects.title: Multi-Region, Multi-Tenant, HA
subjects.why: Production AI must survive AZ loss and noisy neighbors.
subjects.explainer:
Tenancy isolation (keys, quotas, data partitions) prevents noisy-neighbor and leak disasters. HA needs RPO/RTO for model artifacts and indexes, traffic shifting, and degraded modes. Prefix-cache affinity can conflict with naive load balancing — design sticky or replicated caches deliberately.

Common mistake: active-active without index consistency story. Another: one GPU pool for all tenants with no fair-share.

Runbooks beat diagrams when pages fire at 3am.
subjects.project: Design active-active inference across two regions with failover runbook and degraded mode.

topics.title: Tenancy
topics.explainer: Multi-tenant AI systems need isolation in places classic SaaS does not. One heavy tenant can saturate shared GPUs, so use quotas, fair queuing and priority classes. Give each tenant its own keys, budgets and rate limits. Partition data so retrieval filters by tenant at the index level, not in the prompt. Watch for cross-tenant leakage through shared semantic caches, shared memories or fine-tunes trained on mixed data.

topics.title: HA/DR
topics.explainer: Set RPO and RTO for every stateful part: model artifacts, vector indexes, prompt registries, conversation state. Replicate artifacts across regions ahead of time, since pulling 100+ GB of weights during an outage is slow. Use the gateway to shift traffic between regions and providers. Define degraded modes and practice failover in game days. A secondary provider with a different model also needs prompt and eval compatibility, or failover will quietly drop quality.

quiz.q: Sticky routing is sometimes needed to…
quiz.why: Cache locality can dominate latency and cost.

quiz.q: Noisy-neighbor protection on shared GPUs uses…
choices: Quotas, fair queuing and priority classes
quiz.why: These keep one tenant from starving others.

quiz.q: Why pre-replicate model weights to a DR region?
choices: Pulling 100+ GB during an outage is slow
quiz.why: Recovery time depends on artifacts already being there.

subjects.title: Internal AI Platforms
subjects.why: Scale the company by productizing plumbing once.
subjects.explainer:
An internal platform offers model gateway, prompt registry, shared evals, sandbox tool runtime, and cost dashboards as golden paths. Developer experience matters: templates, guardrail defaults, observability out of the box, clear chargeback.

Common mistake: a platform so rigid that squads shadow-IT another vendor. Another: a platform with no product owner — just tickets.

Measure adoption and time-to-first-eval, not only GPU utilization.
subjects.project: Sketch an internal AI platform: registry, eval harness, gateway, sandbox, cost view.

topics.title: Capabilities
topics.explainer: An internal AI platform bundles the things every team would otherwise rebuild: a gateway with routing and budgets, a prompt and configuration registry with versions, a shared evaluation service, a sandboxed tool runtime for agents, and cost dashboards. The goal is that a product team can ship a safe, observable AI feature in days without becoming experts in GPUs or security.

topics.title: Developer Experience
topics.explainer: Platforms succeed through developer experience. Offer golden paths: templates that come with auth, tracing, evals and guardrails already wired. Make safe defaults the easy path. Turn on observability automatically. Make costs visible per team. Prefer self-service with policy guardrails over ticket queues, because teams route around slow platforms and that is how shadow AI starts. Try it: time how long a new team takes from "we want an AI feature" to a traced, budgeted endpoint in staging. If it is weeks, that number is your platform roadmap.

quiz.q: A healthy AI platform optimizes for…
quiz.why: Enable safe speed.

quiz.q: A golden path is…
choices: A template with auth, tracing, evals and guardrails pre-wired
quiz.why: It makes the safe way the easy way.

quiz.q: Shadow AI usually grows when…
choices: The official platform is slow or ticket-driven
quiz.why: Teams route around friction.

subjects.title: Model Cards, Licensing & Procurement
subjects.why: Paperwork is part of the architecture in regulated deals.
subjects.explainer:
Model cards and system cards communicate intended use, limits, and eval summaries. Licensing distinguishes API ToS, open weights, copyleft, and training-data provenance claims. Procurement needs security questionnaires, subprocessors, and exit clauses.

Common mistake: assuming Hugging Face hosting implies a particular license. Another: no plan to extract prompts and evals when switching vendors.

Keep a contract checklist next to the reference architecture.
subjects.project: Fill a model/system card for a client-facing RAG assistant; list license and exit risks.

topics.title: Documentation
topics.explainer: Documentation is how trust scales. Model cards describe what a model is, how it was trained and evaluated, and where it fails. System cards describe the whole application, including prompts, tools, guardrails and human oversight. Publish eval summaries and known limitations honestly. Keep a change log of model and prompt versions so users and auditors can match behavior to releases.

topics.title: Procurement
topics.explainer: Procurement for AI has new details. API terms of service and open-weight licenses differ: check commercial use, user thresholds, and output ownership. List subprocessors and data locations. Prepare for security questionnaires that ask about training on customer data, retention, and isolation. Negotiate exit terms, including data return and deletion. Ask about indemnity for IP claims on outputs, and check whether your insurance covers AI-related incidents.

quiz.q: A model card should include…
choices: Intended use, limits, and evaluation notes
quiz.why: Cards communicate safe use boundaries.

quiz.q: A system card differs from a model card by covering…
choices: The whole application: prompts, tools, guardrails and oversight
quiz.why: Behavior depends on the system, not just the model.

quiz.q: "Open weights" licenses may still…
choices: Restrict commercial use or user counts
quiz.why: Read each license; terms vary widely.

subjects.title: Sovereign & Regulated Architectures
subjects.why: Governments and banks pay for in-boundary designs.
subjects.explainer:
Sovereign AI keeps weights, logs, and often embeddings inside a boundary. Confidential GPUs/TEEs, air-gapped MLOps, signed supply chains, and offline red-team processes appear. Update channels become sneakernet or heavily controlled mirrors.

Common mistake: 'private VPC endpoint to a public model' sold as sovereign. Another: no patch story for CVEs in the serving stack.

Design evidence packs auditors can consume without a live demo.
subjects.project: Design an air-gapped inference plus RAG stack with signed update channel.

topics.title: Controls
topics.explainer: Sovereign and regulated deployments keep weights, prompts, logs and embeddings inside a legal and physical boundary. Confidential computing and GPU TEEs protect data in use from the cloud operator. Evals and red-teaming run inside the boundary too. Models arrive through a signed supply chain with verified hashes. Embedding and search run locally so documents never leave. A private network link to a public model API does not satisfy these requirements on its own.

topics.title: Operations
topics.explainer: Operating inside a boundary changes daily work. Updates arrive as signed bundles, sometimes physically carried in. Break-glass access for emergencies is logged and time-limited. Telemetry must be designed so metrics leave but data does not. Auditors expect evidence packs. Field support may require cleared staff on site, so the support model is part of the architecture, not an afterthought. Try it: write the runbook for a model update that must cross an air gap, from vendor release to signed bundle to production.

quiz.q: A public-model Private Link alone…
choices: Does not make processing fully sovereign
quiz.why: Data still leaves the boundary to the provider.

quiz.q: Confidential computing on GPUs protects data…
choices: In use, even from the host operator
quiz.why: TEEs encrypt memory and attest the environment.

quiz.q: In an air-gapped site, model updates typically arrive as…
quiz.why: Signatures and hashes protect the offline supply chain.

subjects.title: Org Design & AI Transformation
subjects.why: Architecture without operating model fails at handoff.
subjects.explainer:
CoE versus federated versus hub-spoke, platform versus product teams, RACI for model incidents, and hiring skills matrices determine whether designs live. Pilots need explicit scale criteria; vendor sprawl needs governance; executives need metrics beyond demo wow.

Common mistake: centralizing all AI in a team that becomes a bottleneck. Another: federating with zero shared eval standards.

Team Topologies-style thinking maps cleanly onto AI platforms.
subjects.project: Propose CoE plus federated squads for a 2,000-person company adopting agents.

topics.title: Operating Models
topics.explainer: Organizations typically pick a Center of Excellence (central experts), a federated model (each business unit builds), or hub-and-spoke (central platform plus embedded builders). Separate the platform team, which provides paved roads, from product teams, which ship features. Write a RACI for AI incidents. Keep a skills matrix so you know who can do evals, infra, security and domain review. Manage vendors centrally to avoid twenty contracts with the same provider.

topics.title: Change
topics.explainer: Pilots are easy; scaling is hard. Define criteria to graduate a pilot: measured quality, cost per task, security review, owner on call. Watch for shadow AI, where teams use unapproved tools because the official path is slow. Control sprawl by consolidating gateways and prompt stores. Report executive metrics in business terms such as hours saved or resolution rate, and invest in training so staff know what the tools can and cannot do.

quiz.q: A platform team should…
choices: Provide golden paths and reduce cognitive load
quiz.why: Platforms enable; they do not bottleneck forever.

quiz.q: Hub-and-spoke AI organizations combine…
choices: A central platform with builders embedded in business units
quiz.why: The hub provides paved roads; spokes ship domain features.

quiz.q: A good criterion to graduate a pilot is…
choices: Measured quality, cost per task, security review and an on-call owner
quiz.why: Scale needs evidence and ownership.

tracks.name: AI Engineer
tracks.role: Ships AI-powered products: prompts, tools, RAG, evals, APIs, hardening. Day to day: features, golden sets, traces, cost/latency. Differs from Architect (system shape) and Inference (engines): you own the application that calls the model.

subjects.title: LLM Application Fundamentals
subjects.why: Every product starts as messages, tokens, and a reliable client.
subjects.explainer:
Production LLM apps are distributed systems that speak chat APIs. Master streaming SSE, retries with jitter, deadlines, cancellation, and token accounting. Know the difference between chat, completions, and newer responses-style APIs. Structured JSON mode and schema adherence prevent brittle string parsing.

Message design (system/user/assistant/tool) and chat templates are part of the contract with the model. Context budgets are product decisions: what stays, what summarizes, what retrieves.

Common mistake: unbounded retries that amplify outages and bills. Another: blocking the request thread on a 60s model call with no timeout.

Wrap the vendor SDK behind your own client so you can swap providers and add telemetry once.
subjects.project: FastAPI service with streaming chat, retries, timeouts, token accounting, JSON schema mode.

topics.title: Client Craft

subtopics.title: Chat vs completions vs responses APIs

topics.explainer: A solid LLM client handles the boring failures. Know the API shapes: chat completions, newer responses-style APIs with built-in tools and state, and legacy completions. Streaming uses server-sent events; parse incrementally and handle disconnects. Retry 429 and 5xx with exponential backoff and jitter, and use idempotency keys when the call triggers side effects. Set connect and total timeouts and propagate user cancellation so you stop paying for tokens nobody will read. Log input, output and cached token counts on every call so cost is measurable per feature.

topics.title: Message Design
topics.explainer: Messages carry roles (system, user, assistant, tool) that the provider turns into a chat template. Put durable instructions in the system message and task data in user turns. Few-shot examples help most for format and edge cases; keep them short and representative. Budget context explicitly: instructions, retrieved data, history and room for the answer must fit. For multi-turn apps, decide what state you keep server-side versus resend each turn. Providers differ in tool-call formats, max output limits and how they treat system prompts, so wrap them in an adapter.

quiz.q: Streaming primarily improves…
quiz.why: Users see tokens sooner; quality unchanged.

quiz.q: Which errors should a client usually retry with backoff?
quiz.why: Rate limits and transient server errors are retryable; client errors are not.

quiz.q: Propagating user cancellation to the model call mainly saves…
choices: Tokens and money spent on output nobody reads
quiz.why: Generation keeps billing until the request stops.

subjects.title: Prompt & Context Engineering
subjects.why: Most quality gains before fine-tuning live here.
subjects.explainer:
Prompting is specifying behavior under uncertainty. Clear instructions, constraints, schemas, and carefully chosen examples beat purple prose. Context engineering decides what enters the window: system policy, retrieved evidence, tool results, memory summaries — and in what order.

Lost-in-the-middle, recency bias, and compaction loss are practical failure modes. Prefer explicit refusal rules over hoping the model abstains.

Common mistake: a 4,000-word system prompt nobody diffs. Another: stuffing retrieval without citations or overlap checks.

Treat prompts as versioned code with evals on every change.
subjects.project: Take a flaky prompt; add schema, examples, failure modes; measure on 30 cases before/after.

topics.title: Techniques
topics.explainer: Clear prompts state the task, the audience, constraints and the output format, and include an example when format matters. Chain-of-thought helps on multi-step reasoning but costs tokens; reasoning models do it internally, so explicit CoT prompts matter less there. Self-consistency samples several answers and takes the majority, trading cost for accuracy. Use JSON schema or structured output modes instead of begging for JSON. Wrap untrusted content in clear delimiters and tell the model it is data, which helps but does not stop determined injection.

topics.title: Context Engineering
topics.explainer: Context engineering means choosing what goes into the window and in what order. Sources include the system prompt, retrieved documents, memory, tool results and conversation history. Models attend best to the start and end, so put key instructions and the most relevant evidence there. When history grows, compact it by summarizing older turns while pinning facts that must survive. Require citations to retrieved chunks so answers can be verified. Most quality problems in production apps are context problems, not model problems.

quiz.q: Context engineering is mainly about…
choices: What enters the window and in what form
quiz.why: Selection and arrangement of context dominate quality.

quiz.q: Untrusted content in a prompt should be…
quiz.why: Clear boundaries help, though they do not fully stop injection.

quiz.q: Models tend to use information best when it is placed…
choices: At the start or end of the context
quiz.why: "Lost in the middle" degrades recall for centered content.

subjects.title: Tokenizer & Embedding Internals for App Devs
subjects.why: Token and embedding choices silently set cost and recall.
subjects.explainer:
You rarely train a tokenizer, but you must know fertility, multilingual blowups, and how embedding models differ from the chat model. Chunk boundaries that split sentences kill retrieval. Dimension, MRL, and similarity metrics affect index design.

Common mistake: embedding with model A and assuming chat model B 'understands' the same vectors. Another: giant chunks to 'save' embeddings that then exceed useful context.

Measure tokens per page of your real corpus before pricing the product.
subjects.project: Tokenize 20 real docs; report fertility; chunk three ways and compare retrieval hit rate.

topics.title: Tokenizers
topics.explainer: Token counts drive cost, latency and truncation. Measure fertility on your real data: JSON, code, logs and non-English text often tokenize poorly. Special tokens such as end-of-turn markers must never appear in user content unescaped. When text is too long, choose a truncation strategy deliberately (keep the head and tail, summarize the middle, or retrieve) instead of chopping silently. Count tokens with the provider's tokenizer before sending so you can reject or compact oversized requests early.

topics.title: Embeddings
topics.explainer: Embeddings turn text into vectors for search. Bi-encoders embed queries and documents separately, which is fast and indexable; cross-encoders read the pair together and are more accurate, so use them to rerank a shortlist. Matryoshka (MRL) models let you truncate vectors to fewer dimensions with modest quality loss, saving memory. Cosine similarity is standard; normalize vectors so dot product equals cosine. Some models use different prefixes or encoders for queries and documents. Re-evaluate when your domain drifts, and remember that changing embedding models means re-indexing.

quiz.q: A bi-encoder is typically used to…
quiz.why: Bi-encoders enable fast retrieval.

quiz.q: Matryoshka (MRL) embeddings let you…
choices: Truncate vectors to fewer dimensions with modest quality loss
quiz.why: Prefixes of the vector remain useful embeddings.

quiz.q: After L2-normalizing vectors, dot product equals…
quiz.why: Normalization removes magnitude, leaving the cosine.

subjects.title: Tool Calling & Structured I/O
subjects.why: Tools turn chat into software; schemas keep it sane.
subjects.explainer:
Design task-oriented tools with strict schemas and server-side validation. Parallel tool calls, repair turns, max iterations, and human confirmation for irreversible side effects are part of the loop. Error messages back to the model should be actionable, not stack traces with secrets.

Common mistake: exposing 80 CRUD endpoints and wondering why tool selection flails. Another: trusting model-produced SQL without a permission layer.

Fewer, sharper tools beat a mirror of your REST API.
subjects.project: Implement 5 tools with strict schemas, validation, and safe errors back to the model.

topics.title: Design
topics.explainer: Design tools around tasks the model needs, not around your database tables: "refund_order(order_id, reason)" beats generic CRUD. Descriptions are prompts, so write them for the model, with when-to-use guidance and examples. Use strict argument schemas with enums and required fields. Classify side effects as read, reversible write or irreversible write, and make writes idempotent with keys so retries do not double-charge. Return compact, structured results and clear error messages the model can act on.

topics.title: Loop
topics.explainer: The tool loop is: model proposes calls, harness executes, results go back, repeat until the model answers. Run independent calls in parallel. When a tool fails, return a useful error so the model can repair arguments on the next turn rather than crashing. Cap iterations and total tokens so loops cannot run forever. Insert human confirmation before irreversible actions. Give each tool its own timeout so one slow API does not stall the whole run.

quiz.q: Tool results should be treated as…
choices: Untrusted input that can inject instructions
quiz.why: Tool outputs are an injection channel.

quiz.q: Idempotency keys on write tools prevent…
quiz.why: A retried call with the same key is a no-op.

quiz.q: When a tool fails, the harness should…
choices: Return a clear error so the model can repair its call
quiz.why: Actionable errors enable self-correction within budgets.

subjects.title: RAG Systems Deep Dive
subjects.why: Retrieval is the default enterprise grounding path.
subjects.explainer:
Indexing (chunking, embeddings, metadata), hybrid BM25+dense, reranking, query rewrite, multi-hop, and citation grounding form the pipeline. Failures: wrong chunk, split fact, stale index, injection via docs, over-retrieval noise. GraphRAG and knowledge-graph hybrids help when relations matter more than similarity.

Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. Refuse when unsupported.

Common mistake: one-size chunking for policies, tables, and code. Another: no ACL filters on the index in a multi-tenant app.
subjects.project: Hybrid BM25+vector RAG with citations, refusal, ACL filters, and a Ragas-style report.

topics.title: Indexing
topics.explainer: Indexing quality sets the ceiling for RAG. Chunk on structure (headings, sections) rather than fixed character counts, with modest overlap. Pick embeddings by testing retrieval on your data. Attach metadata (source, date, ACL, section) to every chunk so you can filter and cite. Combine BM25 keyword search with dense vectors, since each catches what the other misses. For complex corpora, hierarchical or graph indexes capture relationships that flat chunks lose.

topics.title: Query Path
topics.explainer: At query time, rewrite vague or conversational questions into standalone searches; HyDE generates a hypothetical answer and searches with it. Multi-hop questions need iterative retrieval where each step informs the next. Retrieve broadly (say 50 candidates) then rerank with a cross-encoder down to the best 5 to 10. Force the model to cite chunk ids and to say when the evidence does not cover the question. Good refusals are a feature, not a failure.

topics.title: Failure Modes
topics.explainer: RAG fails in recognizable ways. The answer was split across two chunks and neither alone is enough. The index is stale. A document contains injected instructions that the model follows. Too many weak chunks drown the relevant one. Evals only test easy questions so problems stay hidden. Diagnose by logging retrieved chunks with every answer and labeling failures as retrieval misses versus generation errors; the fixes are completely different.

quiz.q: Hybrid search combines…
quiz.why: Lexical+dense covers complementary failures.

quiz.q: Reranking with a cross-encoder is typically applied to…
quiz.why: Cross-encoders are accurate but too slow for full-corpus search.

quiz.q: To diagnose a bad RAG answer first check…
quiz.why: Separate retrieval misses from generation errors.

subjects.title: Semantic Caching & Gateway Clients
subjects.why: Repeat traffic should not always pay full token price.
subjects.explainer:
Application-level semantic caches and gateway features (LiteLLM and friends) reduce spend on FAQs and repeated agent prefixes. Keys must include tenant, tool policy version, and model identity. Bypass on freshness-critical or personalized paths.

Common mistake: caching answers that include time-varying inventory. Another: sharing cache across permission tiers.

Instrument hit rate next to quality — a high hit rate with wrong answers is a silent outage.
subjects.project: Add a semantic cache with tenant keys; measure hit rate and quality on 100 repeated queries.

topics.title: Design
topics.explainer: Semantic caching stores responses keyed by prompt embeddings and returns a hit when a new prompt is similar enough. The similarity threshold is the main knob: too low and users get wrong answers, too high and nothing hits. Build keys from the embedding plus tenant, model, prompt version and relevant parameters. Use TTLs and event-based invalidation when source data changes. Bypass the cache for personalized or tool-using requests. Expect a cold start with no hits until traffic builds the cache.

topics.title: Ops
topics.explainer: Track hit rate, false-hit rate (sampled and reviewed), latency saved and dollars saved. A poisoned cache, where one bad answer gets served thousands of times, is the classic incident, so keep a way to purge by key pattern instantly. Put the policy version in the key so changes invalidate old entries automatically. In multi-region deployments decide whether caches are regional or replicated. Attribute savings to teams so the value is visible.

quiz.q: Cache keys should change when…
choices: Model, prompt version, or permission scope changes
Only the wall clock changes by 1s
quiz.why: Semantic identity includes policy and model.

quiz.q: The classic semantic-cache incident is…
choices: One wrong answer served thousands of times
quiz.why: Keep the ability to purge entries instantly.

quiz.q: Personalized or tool-using requests should usually…
quiz.why: Their correct answers depend on user-specific state.

subjects.title: Product Evals & Quality Loops
subjects.why: Ship with a gate, not a vibe check.
subjects.explainer:
Suites need capability, safety, and style slices; golden plus adversarial cases; process metrics for tools; cost and latency budgets. Put evals in CI. Calibrate judges. Sample production for new failures.

Common mistake: only happy-path demos in the suite. Another: changing model and prompt simultaneously without a factorial eval.

Make failing evals block merges for critical paths.
subjects.project: CI evals: 40 golden cases; fail PR on >3% quality drop or cost/latency regress.

topics.title: Suite Design
topics.explainer: A product eval suite covers capability (does it solve tasks), safety (refusals, leaks, harmful content) and style (tone, format). Mix golden examples from real traffic with adversarial cases. For agents, add process metrics such as steps taken and tool errors. Track cost and latency per case alongside quality so trade-offs are explicit. Slice results by user cohort, language and task type, because averages hide the segment that is failing.

topics.title: Ops
topics.explainer: Treat evals as code. Version prompts, models and judge configs together so results are reproducible. Calibrate LLM judges against human labels periodically. Sample production traffic into review queues to find new failure types and feed them back into the golden set. Show regression dashboards per release. Quarantine flaky cases and fix their nondeterminism rather than ignoring red results. Try it: run the same eval twice with no changes. Any case that flips is flaky and needs fixing before it can gate a release.

quiz.q: Process metrics for agents include…
choices: Whether the correct tool and args were chosen
quiz.why: Trajectory correctness matters.

quiz.q: Why slice eval results by cohort?
quiz.why: A 90% average can hide a 50% language or task slice.

quiz.q: A case that flips pass/fail with no changes is…
choices: Flaky and should be fixed before gating releases
quiz.why: Flaky cases erode trust in the eval gate.

subjects.title: Vector Search Internals
subjects.why: Retrieval quality and cost depend on how the index actually finds neighbors.
subjects.explainer:
Vector databases use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes such as HNSW, IVF and product quantization. Understanding their knobs lets you trade recall, latency and memory deliberately, size infrastructure, and avoid pitfalls such as filters that destroy recall.

Common mistakes: never measuring recall against exact search; post-filtering ANN results by tenant; re-embedding without re-indexing; choosing a vector DB before knowing data size and filter needs.
subjects.project: Index 1M vectors with HNSW and IVF-PQ in Faiss. Plot recall@10 vs latency for several efSearch and nprobe values, measure memory, then add a tenant filter and observe recall with pre- vs post-filtering.

topics.title: ANN Algorithms
topics.explainer: Exact search is linear in corpus size. HNSW navigates a layered proximity graph and offers excellent recall and latency at the cost of memory (vectors plus links). IVF partitions vectors into clusters and searches only the closest nprobe lists, which is cheaper in memory and easy to shard. Product quantization compresses vectors into compact codes, enabling billions of vectors in RAM, usually with a full-precision rerank of top candidates. DiskANN-style indexes keep most data on SSD.

topics.title: Operating Vector Indexes
topics.explainer: Measure recall@k against exact search on a sample whenever you change parameters or data. Size memory as vectors plus index overhead. Filters by tenant or ACL should be applied during search (filtered HNSW, partitioned indexes) rather than after, or results can come back nearly empty. Plan re-indexing when embedding models change and handle deletes, which some graph indexes support poorly. Hybrid keyword plus vector search is often the best default.

quiz.q: Increasing HNSW efSearch generally…
quiz.why: A wider search explores more candidates.

quiz.q: Product quantization mainly reduces…
quiz.why: Vectors become compact codes.

quiz.q: Post-filtering ANN results by tenant can cause…
choices: Few or no results when the tenant is small
quiz.why: Most top candidates may belong to other tenants.

quiz.q: 10M float32 vectors of 768 dims take about…

subjects.title: Application-Level Agents
subjects.why: When the next step depends on the last result — and only then.
subjects.explainer:
Start with workflows and state machines. Promote to a single tool-using agent when branching is truly model-driven. Use plan-act-observe loops with budgets. Subagents need clear contracts. Deterministic wrappers around brittle steps reduce variance.

Common mistake: a swarm for a form-fill. Another: no stop condition beyond 'model says done.'

Compare agent versus workflow on evals and cost before celebrating autonomy.
subjects.project: Replace a brittle chain with one agent plus tools and stop conditions; compare evals and cost.

topics.title: When to Agent
topics.explainer: Most problems that look like agent problems are workflows: a fixed sequence of steps with an LLM inside some of them. Workflows are cheaper, faster and easier to test. Model the task as a state machine first. Use a single tool-using agent when steps genuinely depend on intermediate results. Only reach for multiple agents when tasks are parallel or need very different contexts. Always define human escalation and step, token and dollar budgets.

topics.title: Implementation
topics.explainer: A practical agent runs plan, act, observe in a loop. A scratchpad or todo list keeps the plan visible across turns. Subagents can handle isolated subtasks with fresh context and return summaries. Wrap fragile operations in deterministic code rather than asking the model to do them. Make every side-effecting tool idempotent so a retry after a crash does not repeat work. Log the full trajectory for debugging and evals.

quiz.q: Prefer a workflow when…
choices: Every step needs creative tool choice
quiz.why: Deterministic pipelines beat agents when known.

quiz.q: Before building multiple agents you should…
choices: Try a workflow, then a single tool-using agent
quiz.why: Complexity should be earned by evidence.

quiz.q: A visible todo list or scratchpad in an agent helps…
choices: Keep the plan coherent across many turns
quiz.why: Explicit plans reduce drift.

subjects.title: Production Hardening
subjects.why: Demos are not products.
subjects.explainer:
Timeouts, circuit breakers, fallback models, queues, backpressure, and idempotent writes keep systems alive. Observability needs structured traces of prompts, tools, tokens, and dollars — with PII redaction. AuthN/Z on tools, output filters, dependency pinning, and spend caps are mandatory.

Common mistake: logging raw prompts to a multi-tenant sink. Another: no kill switch when a prompt change loops tools.

On-call for AI includes quality pages, not only 5xx.
subjects.project: Add tracing, rate limits, spend caps, and a kill switch to your LLM API app.

topics.title: Reliability
