topics.explainer: Production LLM features need the reliability patterns of any distributed system. Set timeouts and circuit breakers on model calls. Configure fallback models or providers. Put async work on queues with backpressure so spikes do not cascade. Make writes idempotent. Shed low-priority load when capacity is short. Test these paths deliberately, because a provider outage is a matter of when, not if.

topics.title: Observability
topics.explainer: Trace every request across retrieval, model calls and tools with structured spans (OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions help). Record tokens, cost, latency and model version per span. Sample outputs for quality review. Alert on drift in quality scores, refusal rates or tokens per request, not only on errors. Redact secrets and personal data before traces are stored, since traces are a common source of leaks.

topics.title: App Security
topics.explainer: Authorize every tool call against the end user's permissions, not the app's service account. Filter outputs for sensitive data and unsafe content before display or action. Redact PII before sending to third-party models where possible. Pin dependency and model versions to avoid supply-chain surprises. Enforce spend caps per user and per key so an abuser or a runaway loop cannot generate a five-figure bill overnight.

quiz.q: A kill switch should be able to…
choices: Disable tools or force safe mode quickly
quiz.why: Operational safety needs fast containment.

quiz.q: Spend caps per user mainly guard against…
choices: Abuse and runaway loops creating huge bills
quiz.why: Hard limits contain the blast radius.

quiz.q: Tool calls should be authorized against…
quiz.why: Otherwise the agent becomes a confused deputy.

subjects.title: Fine-Tuning & Adaptation
subjects.why: Fine-tune when prompting and retrieval hit a ceiling.
subjects.explainer:
SFT for format and style, LoRA/QLoRA for efficient adaptation, DPO-style preference methods when ranked feedback exists. Data quality beats quantity. Watch for catastrophic forgetting and eval before merge. Synthetic data helps if validated against held-out human gold.

Common mistake: fine-tuning to fix retrieval failures. Another: no license review on training data.

Keep a decision record: why fine-tune beat better prompts.
subjects.project: LoRA-tune a small open model on 500 curated examples; compare to prompt+RAG on the same eval.

topics.title: Decision
topics.explainer: Fine-tune only after prompts and retrieval hit a ceiling you can measure. Fine-tuning is good at style, format, narrow skills and making smaller models act like bigger ones; it is bad at teaching fresh facts, which RAG handles better. You need clean, representative data, usually hundreds to thousands of examples. Watch for catastrophic forgetting of general skills. Check that the base model's license allows tuning and your use.

topics.title: Methods
topics.explainer: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains on input-output pairs. LoRA freezes the base model and learns small low-rank matrices, cutting memory and producing swappable adapters; QLoRA does this on a 4-bit base. Preference methods such as DPO, ORPO and KTO learn from chosen-versus-rejected pairs without a separate reward model. Synthetic data can bootstrap training but must be filtered and validated. Always compare the tuned model to the base on your eval suite before merging.

topics.title: Ops
topics.explainer: Version datasets alongside checkpoints. Pick checkpoints by eval score, not by the lowest training loss. Run regression suites that include general capabilities, not just the target task. Keep the previous adapter ready for instant rollback. Budget for refreshes: when the base model gets a new release, you may need to retrain, so automate the pipeline. Try it: keep a one-line rollback command in the runbook and rehearse it, so reverting an adapter takes seconds instead of a meeting.

quiz.q: LoRA adapts models by…
quiz.why: Low-rank adapters are the core idea.

quiz.q: Fine-tuning is a poor choice for…
choices: Distilling a skill into a smaller model
quiz.why: RAG handles fresh facts better; tuning bakes in a snapshot.

quiz.q: DPO trains on…
choices: Pairs of chosen and rejected responses
quiz.why: It optimizes preferences directly without an RL loop.

subjects.title: Synthetic Data & Distillation
subjects.why: Teacher models can mint training fuel — carefully.
subjects.explainer:
Distillation and synthetic data expand scarce labels. Risks: mirroring teacher blind spots, leaking eval contamination, and mode collapse. Prefer diverse generators, critique/filter pipelines, and human spot checks. On-policy data from your own agent traces often beats generic synthetic chat.

Common mistake: training on the same scraped web as the teacher without filters. Another: reporting gains only on synthetic tests.

Always hold out real user-like gold.
subjects.project: Generate synthetic tool-call traces; filter with a critic; train a small student; eval on human gold.

topics.title: Generation
topics.explainer: Synthetic data comes from prompting a strong teacher model to produce examples. Control diversity with varied seeds, personas and topics, or you get thousands of near-duplicates. Filter with critique loops, verifiers, or executable checks such as unit tests. On-policy traces from your own model capture its real mistakes. Check that synthetic items do not overlap your evaluation set, or scores become meaningless.

topics.title: Distillation
topics.explainer: Distillation trains a smaller student to imitate a larger teacher. Logit distillation matches the teacher's full output distribution, which carries more signal than single answers; response distillation trains on teacher outputs only and works with API teachers. Task-specific students can be ten times cheaper with similar quality on that task. Students inherit teacher errors and biases. Plan a refresh cadence as teachers improve.

quiz.q: Synthetic data is safest when…
choices: Filtered and validated against held-out human gold
Used as the only test set
quiz.why: Human gold keeps you honest.

quiz.q: Diversity controls in synthetic data generation prevent…
quiz.why: Varied seeds, personas and topics broaden coverage.

quiz.q: Logit distillation carries more signal than response distillation because…
choices: The student sees the teacher's full probability distribution
quiz.why: Soft targets show how the teacher ranks alternatives.

subjects.title: Multi-Model Routing & Ensembles
subjects.why: Route cheap to expensive; specialize by task.
subjects.explainer:
Heuristic or learned routers, confidence/entropy signals, cascades, and verifiers reduce spend. Best-of-N and critique patterns trade cost for quality. Keep A/B assignment honest.

Common mistake: a router trained on demos that never sees production dialects. Another: cascades without a hard cost ceiling.

Measure dollars and quality together on the same slices.
subjects.project: Build a difficulty router: easy to small model, hard to frontier; report $ and quality.

topics.title: Routing
topics.explainer: Routing sends each request to the cheapest model likely to handle it. Heuristic routers use rules (length, keywords, user tier); learned routers predict difficulty from features. Confidence signals such as logprob entropy or a verifier score can trigger escalation. Cascades try a small model first and defer to a larger one when unsure. Run A/B assignment to measure the quality and cost effect of every routing change.

topics.title: Ensembles
topics.explainer: Ensembles spend more compute for quality. Best-of-N samples several answers and picks the best with a scorer. Verifier models check answers, which works especially well when correctness is checkable (code, math). Debate and critique loops have models review each other. Cap cost per request and keep latency inside the SLO, because ensembles multiply both quickly. Try it: on 100 hard cases, compare single-shot accuracy with best-of-5 plus a verifier, and compute the cost per extra correct answer.

quiz.q: A cascade should…
choices: Stop at the first model that meets a confidence policy
quiz.why: Early exit is the point.

quiz.q: A cascade router escalates to a larger model when…
choices: The small model is uncertain or fails a check
quiz.why: Confidence signals or verifiers trigger deferral.

quiz.q: Best-of-N works best when…
choices: A reliable scorer or verifier exists
quiz.why: Picking the best needs a way to recognize it.

subjects.title: Data Flywheels
subjects.why: Production traffic is training fuel if you instrument it.
subjects.explainer:
Capture consenting, redacted traces; mine failures; queue active learning. Feed eval expansion, SFT, and preference pairs. Close the loop weekly.

Common mistake: storing everything forever without redaction. Another: never promoting production failures into the golden set.

Flywheels need product and legal buy-in, not only ML enthusiasm.
subjects.project: Thumbs and tool-success signals → weekly curated fine-tune and eval delta sets.

topics.title: Capture
topics.explainer: A data flywheel turns usage into improvement. Capture traces only with consent and redaction in place. Mine failures from explicit feedback, user edits, retries and escalations. Use active learning to queue the most informative examples for labeling. Watch sampling bias: users who give feedback are not representative, and you will over-fit to them if you are careless. Try it: list every signal your app already emits (edits, retries, copies, thumbs) and rank them by how strongly they indicate failure.

topics.title: Use
topics.explainer: Captured data feeds several loops: new eval cases, SFT examples, preference pairs from edited or rejected answers, reward signals for RL, and regression tests for prompts. Publish a regular quality report that shows how the flywheel moved key metrics. A flywheel that only collects data without changing the product is just storage cost. Try it: every week, turn the top five new failure clusters into eval cases before anyone changes a prompt. This keeps fixes honest.

quiz.q: A flywheel without redaction…
quiz.why: Traces often contain secrets and PII.

quiz.q: User edits to a draft are valuable because they…
quiz.why: Original vs edited is a chosen/rejected pair.

quiz.q: The main sampling risk in feedback data is…
quiz.why: Bias toward vocal users skews training and evals.

subjects.title: On-Device & Edge Apps
subjects.why: Local models change latency, privacy, and UX.
subjects.explainer:
GGUF/llama.cpp, MLX, ExecuTorch, NPUs, and hybrid local+cloud patterns matter. Cold start, memory budgets, update channels, and honest privacy UX copy are product work.

Common mistake: promising fully offline while still shipping telemetry that needs network. Another: a 7B model that jetsams the OS on mid phones.

Benchmark on target devices, not only your MacBook.
subjects.project: Local RAG demo with llama.cpp or similar; compare quality/latency to cloud on 20 queries.

topics.title: Stack
topics.explainer: Edge apps run quantized models (GGUF via llama.cpp, MLX, ONNX Runtime, Core ML, or vendor NPU runtimes) on CPUs, GPUs or NPUs. Memory is the binding constraint: a 7B model at 4-bit is about 4 GB, before KV cache. Hybrid designs keep simple or private tasks local and send hard ones to the cloud. Plan model update channels with signatures and delta downloads, since models are large.

topics.title: UX
topics.explainer: On-device AI has UX costs. The first load of a model can take seconds. Offline mode should degrade gracefully rather than fail. Tell users plainly what stays on device and what goes to the cloud. Provide degraded modes on low battery or thermal throttling. Measure battery impact; a feature that drains the phone gets uninstalled. Try it: measure cold-start time and battery drain for ten minutes of use on a mid-range phone, not just a flagship.

quiz.q: Edge deployments most improve…
choices: Privacy and latency for suitable workloads
quiz.why: Fit the workload to the device.

quiz.q: A 7B model quantized to 4 bits needs roughly how much memory for weights?
quiz.why: 7B × 0.5 bytes ≈ 3.5 GB plus some overhead.

quiz.q: Hybrid edge designs typically…
choices: Keep simple or private tasks local and escalate hard ones
quiz.why: They balance privacy, latency and capability.

subjects.title: Post-Training Collaboration
subjects.why: Speak research-engineer when prompting is not enough.
subjects.explainer:
Map SFT to preference to RL (RLHF/RLAIF, DPO, GRPO, env-based RL). Understand harness overfitting, reward hacking, and contamination. Know when to request a training run versus change the product.

Common mistake: asking for RL to fix a tool schema bug. Another: optimizing a proxy reward that the agent games.

Bring clean env definitions and evals to the training conversation.
subjects.project: Read a GRPO/DPO report; write a one-pager on product signals that would improve reward.

topics.title: Methods Map
topics.explainer: Post-training turns a base model into an assistant. SFT teaches format and behavior from demonstrations. Preference learning, via RLHF with a reward model or RLAIF with AI feedback, teaches which answers people prefer. DPO, ORPO and KTO do preference learning directly from pairs without the RL loop. GRPO and environment-based RL reward verifiable success, such as passing tests. Distillation copies a stronger model's behavior, often cheaper than RL for narrow goals.

topics.title: Risks
topics.explainer: Training can make things worse. Models over-fit to the harness or eval used in training. Reward hacking finds loopholes, such as editing tests instead of fixing code. Entropy collapse makes outputs repetitive and kills exploration. Contaminated evals hide all of this. Often the right call is not to train at all and instead improve prompts, retrieval or tools. Try it: before approving a training run, write down which prompt, retrieval or tool change you tried first and why it was not enough.

quiz.q: Reward hacking means…
choices: Optimizing the proxy without true task success
quiz.why: The agent games the metric.

quiz.q: GRPO-style RL is especially effective when…
choices: Rewards are verifiable, like passing tests
quiz.why: Verifiable rewards give clean training signals.

quiz.q: Entropy collapse in RL shows up as…
quiz.why: The policy over-concentrates on a few behaviors.

subjects.title: Multimodal Product Engineering
subjects.why: Images, PDFs, and audio change the application contract.
subjects.explainer:
Document AI, screenshot agents, and voice wraps need parsers, size limits, malware scanning, and modality-specific evals. Do not send binaries to a VLM when text extraction suffices.

Common mistake: no max upload or MIME allowlist. Another: evaluating only on clean digital PDFs when users send photos of pages.

Design modality gates in the API, not only in the prompt.
subjects.project: Build an upload path: MIME allowlist, size cap, text-first extraction, VLM fallback, eval set with photos.

topics.title: Pipelines
topics.explainer: Multimodal pipelines should use the cheapest reliable path first: extract text from PDFs and run OCR, and send page images to a VLM only for charts, handwriting or layout-heavy pages. Speech goes through STT before an LLM unless latency demands a native audio model. Screenshots power UI understanding and computer-use agents. Gate inputs by size and MIME type to control cost and attack surface.

topics.title: Eval and Safety
topics.explainer: Each modality needs its own gold data: scanned forms, charts, accents, noisy audio. Test adversarial images, including text hidden in pixels that tries to inject instructions. Scan uploaded files for malware before processing. Accessibility matters too: generated alt text and transcripts should be checked for accuracy, since users may rely on them. Try it: build 20 test images that contain hidden text instructions, and check whether your pipeline obeys any of them.

quiz.q: Prefer text extraction before VLM when…
choices: Digital text PDFs are available and reliable
Every input is a photo of a whiteboard
quiz.why: Cheaper and often more accurate.

quiz.q: A cost-aware document pipeline usually starts with…
choices: Sending every page as an image
Text extraction and OCR, with VLM fallback
quiz.why: Text paths are cheaper and often more accurate.

quiz.q: "Prompt injection in pixels" refers to…
choices: Instructions hidden in images that a VLM may follow
quiz.why: Vision inputs are another untrusted channel.

tracks.name: AI Inference Engineer
tracks.role: Owns tokens/sec, latency SLOs, $/1M tokens. Day to day: engines, KV, batching, speculation, P/D disagg, CUDA profiles. Differs from Infra (clusters) and AI Engineer (apps).

subjects.title: Inference Request Lifecycle
subjects.why: Name stages: tokenize, prefill, decode, detokenize.
subjects.explainer:
Prefill is compute-bound over the full prompt; decode is memory-bound while reading KV. TTFT, ITL/TBT, tokens/s, goodput, queue time, and KV utilization are the dashboard language. Streaming improves perceived latency. Chat templates and tool parsers sit on the critical path — moving render/derender off GPU nodes is an emerging pattern.

Common mistake: maximizing throughput while missing TTFT SLOs. Another: ignoring tokenizer CPU cost on huge batches.

Instrument before you tune.
subjects.project: Local vLLM: log TTFT, ITL, tokens/s, KV utilization for 3 prompt lengths.

topics.title: Stages
topics.explainer: An inference request passes through clear stages. The server applies the chat template and tokenizes. Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel; it is compute-bound and sets time to first token. Decode generates one token per step for every sequence in the batch; it is memory-bandwidth-bound because each step re-reads all weights and the KV cache. Detokenization and tool-call parsing turn ids back into text and structure. Streaming returns tokens as they come; buffering waits for the full output.

topics.title: Metrics
topics.explainer: TTFT (time to first token) measures prefill plus queueing. TBT or ITL (time between tokens) measures decode speed per user. Throughput is tokens per second per GPU across all users. Goodput counts only requests that met their SLOs, which is what actually matters. KV cache hit rate shows how much prefix reuse you get. Queue time reveals under-provisioning before latency explodes. Always report percentiles (p50, p95, p99), not averages.

quiz.q: Prefill is typically…
quiz.why: Full-prompt matmuls dominate.

quiz.q: Decode is usually limited by…
quiz.why: Every step re-reads weights and KV for little compute.

quiz.q: Goodput counts…
choices: Only requests that met their latency SLOs
quiz.why: Throughput that violates SLOs is not useful work.

subjects.title: Serving Engines Landscape
subjects.why: Pick engine for workload, not blog charts.
subjects.explainer:
vLLM (PagedAttention, broad HW), SGLang (RadixAttention, structured out), TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA peak), TGI, llama.cpp for edge. Features differ: prefix cache, speculation, LoRA multiplexing, multimodal.

Common mistake: TRT-LLM without NVIDIA specialization on the team. Another: ignoring observability maturity.

Bake off on YOUR ISL/OSL/concurrency.
subjects.project: Same 7B on vLLM and llama.cpp; compare setup, throughput, features.

topics.title: Open Engines
topics.explainer: vLLM popularized PagedAttention and continuous batching and supports most models and hardware. SGLang adds RadixAttention for automatic prefix reuse and is strong for structured and agentic workloads. TGI is Hugging Face's server. llama.cpp and Ollama run quantized models on CPUs, Macs and small GPUs. Compare on features you need (quantization formats, speculative decoding, LoRA, structured output, disaggregation) and benchmark on your own traffic shape.

topics.title: NVIDIA Stack
topics.explainer: TensorRT-LLM compiles models into optimized engines for NVIDIA GPUs, often the fastest option at the cost of build steps. Triton Inference Server hosts many model types behind one API. NVIDIA Dynamo orchestrates distributed and disaggregated serving with KV-aware routing. NIM packages models as ready-to-run containers. Migrating between stacks costs engineering time, so weigh peak speed against operability. Try it: serve the same model with vLLM and TensorRT-LLM on one GPU and compare tokens per second at concurrency 1, 16 and 64.

quiz.q: RadixAttention shines when…
quiz.why: Prefix reuse wins.

quiz.q: llama.cpp and Ollama are best known for…
choices: Running quantized models on CPUs, Macs and small GPUs
quiz.why: They target local and edge inference.

quiz.q: TensorRT-LLM's main trade-off is…
choices: Peak NVIDIA performance at the cost of build/compile steps
quiz.why: Compiled engines are fast but add pipeline work.

subjects.title: GPU Memory Model for Inference
subjects.why: Weights + KV + activations must fit.
subjects.explainer:
Sizing: parameters times bytes/param plus KV scaling with layers, heads, sequence, batch, precision. PagedAttention treats KV like virtual memory to fight fragmentation.

Common mistake: forgetting KV when estimating 70B fit. Another: huge max_model_len wasting reserved pages.

Back-of-envelope before buying.
subjects.project: Estimate KV bytes for 32B GQA at 8k ctx batch 16; compare to vLLM stats.

topics.title: Fitting
topics.explainer: GPU memory holds weights, KV cache and activations. Weights are parameters times bytes per parameter: 70B at FP16 is 140 GB. KV per token is 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes. Activation peaks happen in prefill of long prompts. Fragmentation wastes memory unless the engine pages it. Engines reserve a fraction of memory up front (for example gpu_memory_utilization 0.9), so nvidia-smi shows "full" even when idle.

topics.title: Techniques
topics.explainer: PagedAttention stores KV in fixed blocks like virtual memory pages, so there is almost no fragmentation and sequences can share prefix blocks. Quantizing KV to FP8 halves its size. Offloading cold KV to CPU memory or NVMe extends effective capacity at a latency cost. Prefix sharing lets requests with the same system prompt reuse KV. Capping max sequence length per tier is a simple and effective policy for protecting memory.

quiz.q: KV scales primarily with…
quiz.why: KV grows with context and concurrency.

quiz.q: Weights of a 70B model in FP16 take about…
quiz.why: 70B × 2 bytes = 140 GB.

quiz.q: nvidia-smi shows a vLLM GPU "full" at idle because…
choices: The engine pre-reserves memory for KV cache
quiz.why: gpu_memory_utilization reserves space up front.

subjects.title: Batching, Scheduling & KV Cache
subjects.why: Continuous batching + paged KV = production.
subjects.explainer:
Static batching waits for the slowest. Continuous/in-flight batching lets finished sequences leave. Chunked prefill reduces TTFT interference. Prefix caching and RadixAttention trees, eviction, quantized KV are levers.

Common mistake: maximizing batch until TBT dies. Another: disabling prefix cache on agent workloads.

Plot throughput-latency Pareto curves.
subjects.project: Saturate GPU; ablate max_num_seqs and max_model_len; plot throughput vs latency.

topics.title: Batching
topics.explainer: Static batching waits for a full batch and holds GPUs until the longest sequence finishes. Continuous batching adds and removes sequences every step, keeping the GPU busy. Chunked prefill splits long prompts into pieces mixed with decode steps so a big prompt does not freeze everyone's token stream. Schedulers can preempt low-priority requests and enforce fairness between tenants. Knobs such as max batched tokens and max sequences trade latency against throughput.

topics.title: KV Cache
topics.explainer: The KV cache stores keys and values for past tokens so decode does not recompute them. Paged blocks manage it efficiently. Prefix caching reuses KV for identical prompt prefixes across requests; RadixAttention organizes cached prefixes as a tree for automatic matching. When memory fills, the engine evicts least-recently-used blocks or preempts sequences. FP8 or INT8 KV roughly doubles capacity with small quality cost on most models.

quiz.q: Continuous batching helps because…
choices: Finished leave and new join without waiting for whole batch
quiz.why: In-flight membership raises utilization.

quiz.q: Chunked prefill prevents…
choices: Long prompts from stalling other users' token streams
quiz.why: Splitting prefill lets decode steps interleave.

quiz.q: Prefix caching benefits most when…
choices: Many requests share a long system prompt or document
quiz.why: Shared prefixes reuse KV blocks.

subjects.title: Quantization for Serving
subjects.why: Bits → memory → batch → money.
subjects.explainer:
Weight quant (INT8/4, GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF), FP8, activation smoothing, KV quant trade quality for capacity. Calibration sets matter. Know when quality collapses on YOUR eval.

Common mistake: INT4 on safety classifiers. Another: English-only quality checks.

A/B on task gold.
subjects.project: Serve large model AWQ/FP8; compare quality on 50 prompts vs higher precision.

topics.title: Weight Quant
topics.explainer: Weight quantization stores weights in fewer bits. GPTQ and AWQ produce INT4 weights with small accuracy loss using a calibration set; GGUF is llama.cpp's format with many variants. FP8 on Hopper and newer GPUs keeps quality very close to BF16 with hardware support. Calibrate on data like your traffic. Per-channel or group scales handle outlier columns. Always re-run your evals after quantizing, because averages can hide broken edge cases.

topics.title: Activations & KV
topics.explainer: Activations and KV are harder to quantize than weights because of outliers, a few huge values in certain channels. SmoothQuant shifts that difficulty from activations into weights. KV FP8 is widely supported and usually safe. Symptoms of quantization collapse include repetition, broken formatting and wrong math. Mixed schemes keep sensitive layers in higher precision while quantizing the rest. Try it: enable FP8 KV cache, rerun your eval, and compare both quality and the maximum concurrent sequences the engine reports.

quiz.q: Main serving win from quant is usually…
choices: Higher effective batch from lower memory
quiz.why: Memory→batch→throughput/$.

quiz.q: FP8 serving requires…
choices: Hardware support such as Hopper or newer
quiz.why: Native FP8 Tensor Core support makes it fast.

quiz.q: After quantizing a model you must…
quiz.why: Averages can hide broken edge cases.

subjects.title: Speculative Decoding
subjects.why: Memory-bound decode; speculation helps at small batch.
subjects.explainer:
Draft models, EAGLE/Medusa, n-gram, MTP, tree verification raise tokens per expensive forward when acceptance is high. Gains shrink at high batch. Measure acceptance by position.

Common mistake: expecting miracles on saturated high-batch servers. Another: ignoring draft quality drift.

Benchmark batch 1/8/32.
subjects.project: Enable EAGLE or draft speculation; measure speedup at batch 1/8/32.

topics.title: Methods
topics.explainer: Speculative decoding guesses several tokens cheaply and verifies them in one pass of the big model. A small draft model can propose tokens. EAGLE and Medusa add lightweight heads to the target model. N-gram lookup copies spans from the prompt, great for editing and RAG. Multi-token prediction (MTP) trains the model to predict ahead. Tree verification checks several candidate branches at once. Output distribution stays the same as the target model when done correctly.

topics.title: Limits
topics.explainer: Speedup depends on acceptance rate: how often the target agrees with the draft. Predictable text (code, templated output) accepts well; creative text less so. At large batch sizes the GPU is already busy, so verification overhead can erase the gain. The draft model costs memory and compute too. Benchmark at your real concurrency and tune the number of speculated tokens.

quiz.q: Speculation helps most when…
quiz.why: Memory-bound decode + accepts = wins.

quiz.q: Speculative decoding preserves output quality because…
choices: The target model verifies every accepted token
quiz.why: Rejection sampling keeps the target distribution.

quiz.q: N-gram lookup speculation works especially well for…
choices: Editing and RAG where outputs copy prompt spans
quiz.why: Copied spans are easy to predict from the prompt.

subjects.title: Structured Output & Constrained Decode
subjects.why: JSON mode has perf tradeoffs.
subjects.explainer:
FSM/grammar masking, tool-call parsers, token healing keep outputs valid. Grammar compile cost and cache interactions matter.

Common mistake: regex on unconstrained dumps. Another: recompiling grammars per request.

Validity rate is an SLO.
subjects.project: Benchmark unconstrained vs grammar JSON; measure tokens/s and validity.

topics.title: Techniques
topics.explainer: Constrained decoding compiles a JSON schema or grammar into a state machine and masks invalid tokens at each step, so output always parses. Token healing fixes boundary issues where the prompt ends mid-token. Partial JSON repair helps clients that parse streams. Tool-call parsers extract function calls from model-specific formats. Version schemas, since changing a schema can change model behavior. Try it: generate 1,000 outputs with and without schema constraints and count parse failures. The difference is usually dramatic.

topics.title: Ops
topics.explainer: Grammar compilation costs time, so cache compiled schemas. Constraints can interact with prefix caching and speculative decoding in engine-specific ways. Failure modes include the model being forced into valid but wrong values, or long loops of whitespace. Agree on contracts with clients about required fields and error handling. Monitor schema violation and repair rates. Try it: log time spent compiling grammars per request; if it is large, cache compiled schemas by hash.

quiz.q: Constrained decoding enforces…
quiz.why: Masked logits implement grammar.

quiz.q: Constrained decoding guarantees…
choices: Syntactically valid output for the schema
quiz.why: Valid structure, not necessarily true content.

quiz.q: Grammar compilation cost is best handled by…
quiz.why: Repeated schemas then cost nothing to compile.

subjects.title: Prefill/Decode Disaggregation
subjects.why: Long prompts stall decodes; split when justified.
subjects.explainer:
Co-located serving couples FTL and TBT. P/D disagg separates pools, transfers KV, rate-matches capacity. Bidirectional KV helps multi-turn.

Common mistake: disaggregating low-ISL chat where co-location wins. Another: ignoring transfer bandwidth.

SLA-aware planners beat static ratios.
subjects.project: Minimal P/D split or simulation; compare TTFT/TBT under long-ISL load.

topics.title: Motivation
topics.explainer: Prefill is compute-heavy and bursty; decode is memory-bound and steady. On shared GPUs, a large prefill stalls ongoing decodes (interference), hurting time between tokens. Disaggregation runs them on separate GPU pools sized for each phase, so you can match the prefill-to-decode ratio to your input and output lengths. It wins for long inputs and strict latency SLOs; for short prompts and small deployments, co-location is simpler and cheaper.

topics.title: Implementation
topics.explainer: In a disaggregated setup, a router sends a request to a prefill worker, which computes the KV cache and transfers it to a decode worker over NVLink or RDMA (NIXL, Mooncake and similar libraries do this). The proxy coordinates handoff and streaming. Capacity planning sets the ratio of prefill to decode GPUs. New failure modes include stuck KV transfers and imbalance between pools, so monitor transfer latency and queue depth on both sides.

topics.title: Frameworks & Operations
topics.explainer: Several stacks now ship disaggregated serving: vLLM and SGLang support separate prefill and decode instances with KV connectors, NVIDIA Dynamo adds KV-aware routing and the NIXL transfer library, llm-d brings it to Kubernetes, and Mooncake pioneered a KV-cache-centric design. Operating them means monitoring KV transfer latency and failures, the ratio of prefill to decode capacity, and queueing on each side. Start with co-located serving, measure interference, and move to disaggregation only when TBT SLOs demand it.

quiz.q: P/D disagg targets…
choices: Interference between long prefills and ongoing decodes
quiz.why: Stage separation reduces cross-SLO interference.

quiz.q: Co-located prefill and decode is usually better for…
choices: Very long inputs with strict TBT
quiz.why: Disaggregation adds KV transfer and orchestration overhead.

quiz.q: In P/D disaggregation the KV cache is…
choices: Transferred from prefill to decode workers
quiz.why: Transfer over NVLink/RDMA avoids recomputation.

subjects.title: Distributed Inference Parallelism
subjects.why: Bigger than one GPU needs a plan.
subjects.explainer:
Tensor, pipeline, expert (MoE), sequence/context parallelism. NCCL, NVLink/NVSwitch, IB/RoCE, overlap decide scale-out value.

Common mistake: TP across nodes without bandwidth. Another: EP without load-balance monitors.

NCCL tests are bring-up.
subjects.project: Serve TP=2 and TP=4; explain bottlenecks; note when PP/EP helps.

topics.title: Types
topics.explainer: When a model does not fit on one GPU, split it. Tensor parallelism splits each layer's matrices across GPUs and needs fast all-reduce, so keep it within an NVLink domain. Pipeline parallelism assigns layers to stages, tolerating slower links but adding bubbles. Expert parallelism places MoE experts on different GPUs with all-to-all routing. Sequence or context parallelism splits very long sequences. Large deployments combine them.

topics.title: Communication
topics.explainer: Distributed inference lives or dies on communication. NCCL provides collectives such as all-reduce and all-to-all. NVLink and NVSwitch give hundreds of GB/s inside a node or rack; InfiniBand or RoCE connect nodes at lower bandwidth. Good engines overlap communication with compute. Place tensor-parallel groups inside the fastest domain and check the topology with nvidia-smi topo -m before blaming the model.

quiz.q: Tensor parallelism shards…
choices: Matmuls across GPUs for one replica
quiz.why: TP splits layer math.

quiz.q: Pipeline parallelism tolerates slower links but adds…
quiz.why: Stages idle while waiting for micro-batches.

quiz.q: Expert parallelism mainly generates which collective?
quiz.why: Tokens are dispatched to experts on other GPUs and gathered back.

subjects.title: Multi-LoRA & Adapter Serving
subjects.why: Many customers, one base.
subjects.explainer:
Multi-LoRA batching hosts many adapters with request routing. Memory, hot-swap, noisy-neighbor need policy.

Common mistake: thousands of cold adapters in GPU memory. Another: no tenant rate isolation.

Adapters are first-class deployables.
subjects.project: Serve two LoRAs on one vLLM; measure switch overhead and isolation.

topics.title: Memory & Routing
topics.explainer: Multi-LoRA serving keeps one base model in memory and loads many small adapters. Adapters are megabytes to hundreds of megabytes each. The router sends each request to a server that has its adapter loaded; hot adapters stay in GPU memory, cold ones live in CPU or disk. Kernels such as Punica and S-LoRA batch requests with different adapters together. Quantized adapters save more memory.

topics.title: Ops
topics.explainer: Treat adapters as deployable artifacts with versions. Canary new adapters on a slice of traffic. A heavily used adapter can starve others, so enforce fairness. Keep rollback instant by retaining the previous version. Emit metrics per adapter (latency, errors, quality) so tenant-specific problems are visible. A useful rule: an adapter is a release, not a file. Give it a version, an owner, an eval report and a rollback path. Try it: serve two adapters on one base model and route by request header, watching latency per adapter.

quiz.q: Multi-LoRA aims to…
choices: Host many adapters on one base engine
quiz.why: Specialization without full replicas.

quiz.q: Multi-LoRA serving keeps…
choices: One base model plus many small adapters
quiz.why: Adapters share the base weights.

quiz.q: Cold adapters typically live in…
choices: CPU memory or disk until requested
quiz.why: Hot ones are promoted to GPU memory.

subjects.title: Weight Loading & Cold Start
subjects.why: Autoscaling LLMs fails if a new replica takes ten minutes to become ready.
subjects.explainer:
A new replica must get a node, pull an image, load tens to hundreds of GB of weights, initialize the engine and warm up. Each step can be measured and shortened. This subject covers where time goes, fast loading techniques, and how to choose between always-on, warm pools and scale-to-zero per model.

Common mistakes: pulling weights from object storage on every start; huge images with weights baked in and no layer caching; autoscaling on signals that react too late for a minutes-long cold start.
subjects.project: Measure each cold-start phase for a 7B-70B model: node ready, image pull, weight load (object store vs local NVMe vs streamer), engine init, first token. Then cut total time by at least half and document which change mattered most.

topics.title: Where the Time Goes
topics.explainer: Break cold start into phases and time each: node provisioning (cloud can take minutes), image pull (CUDA images are often 10+ GB), weight download and load into GPU memory (model bytes ÷ bandwidth), engine initialization (KV cache allocation, CUDA graph capture, kernel compilation such as torch.compile), and warmup requests. Without measurement, teams optimize the wrong phase. Log timestamps for each phase on every start and keep the distribution, not just one run.

topics.title: Fast Loading Techniques
topics.explainer: Shorten the big phases. Keep weights on node-local NVMe or a shared high-throughput cache rather than object storage. Use safetensors so tensors can be memory-mapped and streamed. Stream tensors concurrently straight to GPU memory. Pre-shard checkpoints to your tensor-parallel layout so each GPU reads only its slice. Keep images slim and pre-pulled on nodes; use lazy-loading image formats. Cache compiled artifacts (CUDA graphs, compile caches) where your engine supports it.

topics.title: Scale-to-Zero vs Warm Pools
topics.explainer: Every model needs a readiness policy. Hot models stay always-on with headroom. Warm models keep a small pool of ready replicas and scale out from there. Cold models scale to zero and accept a first-request delay, shown honestly in the UI. Scale on leading signals (queue depth, request rate trends) and pre-scale for known peaks. For multi-model platforms, multiplex many rarely used models or LoRA adapters on shared replicas instead of dedicating GPUs to each.

quiz.q: Time to load 140 GB of weights at 7 GB/s is about…
quiz.why: 140 ÷ 7 = 20 seconds.

quiz.q: Pre-sharding checkpoints to the TP layout helps because…
choices: Each GPU reads only its slice
quiz.why: Less data per GPU, loaded in parallel.

quiz.q: Scale-to-zero is a good fit for…
choices: Rarely used models where a first-request delay is acceptable
quiz.why: Savings outweigh occasional cold starts.

quiz.q: Why is safetensors faster to load than pickle checkpoints?
choices: It can be memory-mapped without code execution
quiz.why: Raw tensor layout enables zero-copy mapping.

subjects.title: LLM Gateways & Inference Routing
subjects.why: Routing decides cost, latency and resilience before a single token is generated.
subjects.explainer:
Gateways give every app one endpoint with keys, budgets, policy and traces, and route across providers, models and replicas. Inside a self-hosted fleet, KV- and prefix-aware routing can cut prefill work dramatically. This subject covers gateway functions, endpoint picking, and multi-model policies.

Common mistakes: round-robin across LLM replicas; fallbacks to models never evaluated with your prompts; gateways without per-tenant budgets.
subjects.project: Put LiteLLM or Envoy AI Gateway in front of two self-hosted replicas and one external provider. Add per-team budgets and a fallback. Then compare round-robin against prefix-aware routing on a workload with a shared 4k-token system prompt, measuring TTFT and GPU prefill time.

topics.title: Gateway Functions
topics.explainer: A production gateway terminates auth, maps virtual keys to provider keys, enforces rate limits and budgets per team, normalizes request formats, runs policy hooks (PII redaction, injection screening, content rules), applies retries, fallbacks and hedging, and emits traces with tokens and cost. It is also where you implement model aliases ('support-default' points to a specific model version) so apps never hard-code model names.

topics.title: KV- and Prefix-Aware Routing
topics.explainer: LLM replicas are stateful: each holds a KV cache. A smart endpoint picker scores replicas on queue length, KV utilization, loaded LoRA adapters and prefix-cache affinity, sending requests that share a prefix to the replica that already cached it. This avoids recomputing long system prompts and documents. Balance affinity with load to avoid hot spots. The Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension standardizes this pattern; llm-d and Dynamo implement it with cache-aware schedulers.

topics.title: Multi-Model & Multi-Provider Policy
topics.explainer: Routing policy decides which model serves a request: by tier, task, cost budget, region or a learned difficulty score. Fallback chains handle provider outages and rate limits. Every target in a chain must be evaluated with your prompts, or failover silently lowers quality. Log the routing decision with each request so cost and quality can be attributed. Review policies regularly as prices and models change.

quiz.q: Prefix-aware routing saves mainly…
choices: Prefill compute for shared prompt prefixes
quiz.why: Cached KV for the prefix is reused.

quiz.q: Model aliases in a gateway let you…
choices: Swap the underlying model without app changes
quiz.why: Apps call a stable name.

quiz.q: A fallback model that was never evaluated with your prompts risks…
quiz.why: Prompts tuned for one model may fail on another.

quiz.q: Why is round-robin a poor fit for LLM replicas?
choices: It ignores KV state, queue depth and cached prefixes
quiz.why: Replicas are stateful and unevenly loaded.

subjects.title: GPU Kernels & Attention Impls
subjects.why: Profiles and sometimes Triton.
subjects.explainer:
FlashAttention IO-aware algorithm, GQA/MQA paths, paged kernels, MLA variants. Nsight, Triton, CUDA graphs, torch.compile.

Common mistake: 'faster' kernels ignoring numerics. Another: microbenchmarks that vanish under continuous batching.

Read the profile first.
subjects.project: Profile attention; write small Triton fused op; compare to PyTorch.

topics.title: Attention Kernels
topics.explainer: FlashAttention computes attention in tiles that stay in fast on-chip SRAM, avoiding writing the huge score matrix to HBM; it is exact, just IO-aware. GQA and MQA kernels exploit shared KV heads. Paged attention kernels read KV from scattered blocks. MLA variants decompress latent KV on the fly. Numeric modes (BF16, FP8) change speed and accuracy, and newer GPUs add special instructions for them.

topics.title: Tooling
topics.explainer: Profile before optimizing. Nsight Systems shows the timeline of kernels, copies and gaps; Nsight Compute digs into one kernel. Triton lets you write custom GPU kernels in Python. CUDA graphs remove CPU launch overhead, which matters a lot in decode. torch.compile fuses operations automatically. The roofline model tells you whether a kernel is limited by compute or memory bandwidth, and therefore which optimization can help.

quiz.why: IO-aware tiling cuts HBM trips.

quiz.q: CUDA graphs mainly reduce…
quiz.why: Replaying captured graphs avoids per-kernel launch cost, important in decode.

quiz.q: The roofline model tells you whether a kernel is…
quiz.why: That decides which optimizations can help.

subjects.title: Capacity Planning & SLO Engineering
subjects.why: Inference is SRE with GPUs.
subjects.explainer:
Load shapes, concurrency vs batch, autoscale signals, warm pools, admission control, shedding, fallbacks, priority lanes.

Common mistake: autoscaling on CPU while GPUs bottleneck. Another: no overload playbook.

Write runbooks while calm.
subjects.project: Size GPUs for a latency SLO with headroom; write overload runbook.

topics.title: Planning
topics.explainer: Capacity planning starts with load shape: requests per second, input and output lengths, and how bursty traffic is. Concurrency is not batch size; many concurrent users can be served by continuous batching on few GPUs until KV memory runs out. Autoscale on queue depth or tokens in flight, not CPU. Keep warm pools because cold starts on GPUs take minutes. Hold headroom for spikes and failures.

topics.title: Degradation
topics.explainer: When demand exceeds capacity, degrade on purpose. Admission control rejects or queues requests before they hurt everyone. Shed non-critical traffic such as batch jobs first. Fall back to a smaller model for some tiers. Use priority lanes so paying or interactive users keep their SLOs. Communicate clearly during incidents, including status pages, because silent slowness erodes trust faster than an honest message.

quiz.why: SLO-compliant useful work.

quiz.q: GPU serving should autoscale on…
choices: Queue depth or tokens in flight
quiz.why: CPU barely moves when GPUs saturate.

quiz.q: Warm pools exist because…
choices: GPU cold starts (node + image + weights) take minutes
quiz.why: Spikes cannot wait for cold capacity.

subjects.title: Next-Gen Hardware & Memory Systems
subjects.why: GB200-class and offload change designs.
subjects.explainer:
Blackwell/GB200, AMD MI300/ROCm, hybrid CPU+GPU, other accelerators, HBM limits, KV offload, CXL, multi-host KV.

Common mistake: interconnect-light hardware for heavy TP/EP. Another: ignoring power/cooling in BOM.

Briefs tied to traffic mix.
subjects.project: Design brief: NVLink-heavy vs many smaller GPUs for your ISL/OSL mix.

topics.explainer: Hardware sets serving economics. NVIDIA Blackwell and GB200 NVL72 racks connect 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain, ideal for big MoE models. AMD Instinct GPUs with ROCm offer large HBM and are supported by major engines. CPU-plus-GPU superchips share memory coherently. Other accelerators (TPUs, Trainium, Gaudi, inference ASICs) can be cheaper for supported models. Power per rack is now a first-class constraint.

topics.title: Memory
topics.explainer: HBM capacity decides how many sequences and how much context fit; HBM bandwidth decides decode speed. KV offload to CPU or NVMe and CXL memory pools extend capacity. Multi-host KV stores let any server reuse cached prefixes. Each extra tier adds latency and new failure domains, so measure hit rates before adding complexity. Try it: compute how many 8k-token sequences fit in the KV budget of your GPU, then compare with what the engine logs at startup.

subjects.title: Inference Research Watchlist
subjects.why: Papers become engine features fast.
subjects.explainer:
Better speculation, learned schedulers, cross-request memory, energy-aware serving, MoE placement. Follow MLSys and engine roadmaps.

Common mistake: adopting a paper before the bottleneck matches. Another: never revisiting quarterly.

Tag reading: try/watch/ignore.
subjects.project: Pick one recent inference paper; reproduce a figure or toy the idea.

topics.title: Active Topics
topics.explainer: Inference research moves monthly. Watch better speculation methods, learned schedulers that predict output length, cross-request KV sharing at cluster scale, energy-aware serving that trades a little latency for power, smarter MoE expert placement, and new variants of disaggregation. Before adopting a paper, check whether the gains hold at your batch sizes, models and hardware, and whether a maintained engine already implements it.

tracks.name: AI Infrastructure
tracks.role: Owns GPU platform: clusters, scheduling, storage, networking, observability, cloud. Differs from Inference (engines) and Architect (solution design).

subjects.title: GPU Architecture Literacy
subjects.why: Schedule devices you understand.
subjects.explainer:
SMs, HBM, L2, Tensor Cores, numeric formats, MIG/MPS, power/thermals. Drivers, CUDA/ROCm, container toolkits.

Common mistake: GPU util without HBM/SM clocks. Another: CUDA version skew across nodes.

nvidia-smi and DCGM are literacy.
subjects.project: Collect metrics under idle/prefill/decode loads; explain differences.

topics.title: Hardware
topics.explainer: A GPU is many streaming multiprocessors (SMs) sharing an L2 cache and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Tensor Cores do the matrix math, fastest in low-precision formats such as BF16, FP8 and FP4. HBM size limits what fits; HBM bandwidth limits decode speed. MIG splits one GPU into isolated slices; MPS lets processes share SMs concurrently. GPUs throttle when hot or power-capped, so clocks matter as much as utilization. Learn the failure modes too: ECC errors, fallen-off-the-bus events, and NVLink errors.

topics.title: Software
topics.explainer: The software stack goes kernel driver, CUDA (or ROCm) runtime, libraries such as cuDNN, cuBLAS and NCCL, then frameworks. The NVIDIA Container Toolkit exposes GPUs to containers. CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES controls which GPUs a process sees. The classic production bug is version skew: a container built for a newer CUDA than the node's driver supports, or different driver versions across nodes in one training job. Pin and inventory versions everywhere.

subjects.title: Kubernetes for Accelerators
subjects.why: K8s + device plugins is the default platform.
subjects.explainer:
Device plugins, GPU Operator, quotas, taints/affinities, DRA. Jobs vs Deployments vs Ray. Model pull init containers; PVC vs NVMe; pod security.

Common mistake: YAML asks for 1 GPU, runtime sees 0. Another: no split between train and serve nodes.

Golden images beat snowflakes.

topics.title: Devices
topics.explainer: Kubernetes sees GPUs through device plugins that advertise resources like nvidia.com/gpu. The NVIDIA GPU Operator installs and manages the driver, container toolkit, device plugin, DCGM exporter, MIG manager and feature discovery as one unit. Use ResourceQuotas to cap GPUs per namespace, and taints plus node affinity to keep non-GPU pods off expensive nodes. Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) is the newer API for richer device requests.

topics.title: Workloads
topics.explainer: Training fits Jobs (or JobSet, Kubeflow Training Operator, or Ray via KubeRay); serving fits Deployments behind autoscalers. Model weights are large, so pull them with init containers or sidecars, or mount a shared volume or cache to avoid every pod downloading 100 GB. EmptyDir on local NVMe is fast scratch; PVCs persist. Apply pod security standards even to GPU workloads, and use PriorityClasses so production serving can preempt experiments.

topics.title: Day-2 GPU Cluster Ops
topics.explainer: Running GPU clusters day to day means planned driver upgrades with drains, node health checks before scheduling, labeling nodes by GPU model and health, autoscaling node pools, and keeping spare capacity for failures. Track allocatable versus used GPUs per namespace to spot waste. Keep runbooks for stuck pods holding GPUs and for nodes whose device plugin stopped advertising devices. Most outages here are slow leaks, not explosions.

subjects.why: The layer that pages you.
subjects.explainer:
cgroups, hugepages, IOMMU, persistence mode, fabric manager, runtime hooks, secure base images. Debug 'GPU not found' in five minutes.

Common mistake: upgrading driver under pinned CUDA userspace. Another: writable root + host GPU in multi-tenant clusters.

Exact-command runbooks.

topics.title: OS/Driver
topics.explainer: GPU nodes need care at the OS layer. Enable persistence mode so the driver stays loaded and first calls are not slow. NVSwitch systems require the Fabric Manager service, or multi-GPU jobs fail. Match driver and CUDA userspace per NVIDIA's compatibility matrix. IOMMU and PCIe ACS settings can silently cut peer-to-peer bandwidth. Run health checks (DCGM diagnostics) at boot and periodically to catch bad GPUs before jobs land on them.

topics.title: Containers
topics.explainer: Containers reach GPUs through runtime hooks (the NVIDIA Container Toolkit or CDI) that mount device files and driver libraries. Avoid privileged containers; mount only needed devices. Keep seccomp and AppArmor profiles on. Pin images by digest so a tag update cannot change your CUDA stack overnight. Scan images, since AI images are huge and pull in many dependencies. Try it: run nvidia-smi inside an unprivileged container with only the needed device mounted, and confirm it works without --privileged.

topics.title: Batch/Train
topics.explainer: Slurm still runs most HPC and many training clusters: partitions group nodes, GRES describes GPUs, and fairshare balances users. Gang scheduling starts all pods of a distributed job together or none at all, preventing deadlock where half a job holds GPUs waiting for the rest. Preemption reclaims GPUs for higher priority work, so jobs must checkpoint. Reservations hold capacity for planned runs.

topics.title: Serving
topics.explainer: Serving autoscalers should scale on queue depth, tokens per second, or KV usage, not CPU. Kueue adds job queueing, quotas and fair sharing across teams on Kubernetes; Volcano offers gang scheduling and batch policies. KubeRay manages Ray clusters for serving and training. Binpacking fills nodes tightly to free whole nodes; spreading improves resilience. Spot GPUs need graceful drain and fast restart.

subjects.why: Weight distribution dominates cold start.
subjects.explainer:
Object stores, parallel FS, NVMe scratch, registries, P2P/lazy pulls, dataset streaming, index DR. Immutable versioned artifacts.

Common mistake: pulling 70B remotely on every scale-up. Another: mutable latest tags.

Cold-start budget is an SLO.

topics.title: Systems
topics.explainer: Object storage (S3 and equivalents) holds checkpoints and datasets cheaply but with high latency. Parallel file systems (Lustre, GPFS, WEKA, VAST) feed training at high throughput. Local NVMe gives the fastest scratch and model cache. Container and model registries store versioned artifacts. Vector indexes have their own storage needs, mostly RAM and SSD. Rule of thumb: object store for durability, parallel FS for training throughput, local NVMe for hot model cache. Try it: time loading the same checkpoint from each tier on one node.

topics.title: Patterns
topics.explainer: Store models and datasets as immutable, versioned artifacts with hashes. Speed up cold starts with peer-to-peer distribution, lazy-loading image formats, or node-local caches. Stream datasets instead of copying them to every node. Back up checkpoints across regions. Plan bandwidth: 100 nodes each pulling a 140 GB model at once is 14 TB of traffic. Try it: measure cold-start time for a 70B model pulled from object storage versus a node-local cache, and put both numbers in your capacity plan.

subjects.title: High-Performance Networking
subjects.why: Distributed AI dies on bad fabric.
subjects.explainer:
NVLink/NVSwitch, PCIe, IB, RoCE, GPUDirect, NCCL knobs, topology-aware placement. Interpret NCCL busbw vs algbw.

Common mistake: RoCE without lossless config. Another: ignoring PCIe topology.

Fabric is in the BOM.
subjects.project: Run NCCL all-reduce tests; document topology and bandwidth.

topics.title: Fabrics
topics.explainer: Inside a server, NVLink and NVSwitch connect GPUs at hundreds of GB/s, far above PCIe. Between servers, InfiniBand gives low latency and lossless transport; RoCE runs RDMA over Ethernet but needs careful congestion control (PFC and ECN). New AI Ethernet NICs and switches aim to match InfiniBand. PCIe topology matters: a GPU and NIC on different CPU sockets cross a slow link.

topics.title: Libraries/Ops
topics.explainer: NCCL picks algorithms and transports automatically, but environment variables such as NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME and NCCL_IB_HCA reveal and control its choices. GPUDirect RDMA lets NICs read GPU memory directly, skipping the CPU. Topology-aware placement keeps communicating ranks close. Packet loss shows up as slow or hung collectives, not errors. Monitor link counters and run nccl-tests regularly. Try it: run nccl-tests all_reduce_perf across two nodes with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and confirm the log shows the InfiniBand or RoCE transport, not TCP sockets.

quiz.why: Collectives ride the fabric.

quiz.q: RoCE requires careful configuration of…
choices: Congestion control such as PFC and ECN
quiz.why: RDMA over Ethernet needs a well-behaved lossless or near-lossless fabric.

quiz.q: If NCCL logs show it fell back to TCP sockets on an InfiniBand cluster, you should…
choices: Check NCCL_IB_HCA, drivers and RDMA device visibility
quiz.why: Socket fallback cuts bandwidth dramatically.

subjects.why: Capacity is a market.

Reservations, spot, secondary clouds, owned depreciation, lead times, SKU fit to parallelism.

Quarterly plans beat panic buys.

topics.title: Buying
topics.explainer: GPUs come through on-demand cloud, reservations and committed-use discounts, spot instances, newer GPU clouds, or owned hardware. Reservations trade flexibility for price and availability guarantees. Spot is cheap but can disappear at any moment. Owned hardware has the lowest unit cost at high utilization, but lead times for GPUs, power and data center space can run many months. Try it: model one year of a steady workload on on-demand, one-year reserved and spot-with-fallback pricing, including the cost of interruptions.

topics.title: Fit
topics.explainer: Pick hardware for the workload. Large models need enough HBM per GPU or per NVLink domain. Training and tensor-parallel serving need high-bandwidth interconnect SKUs. Check power and cooling: modern racks can exceed 100 kW and need liquid cooling. Confirm your software stack supports the accelerator. Consider lock-in to one vendor's ecosystem when committing for years. Try it: for a target model, write the minimum GPU memory, interconnect and rack power needed, then check which offerings in your region meet all three.

subjects.title: GPU Interconnects & Collective Debugging
subjects.why: Most multi-GPU slowdowns are communication problems, not compute problems.
subjects.explainer:
Inside a node, GPUs talk over NVLink/NVSwitch; between nodes, over InfiniBand or RoCE with GPUDirect RDMA. NCCL turns that fabric into collectives (all-reduce, all-gather, all-to-all). Your job is to know the expected bandwidth of every hop, prove it with nccl-tests, and recognize when a job is slow because a link, NIC binding or transport choice is wrong.

Common mistakes: tensor parallelism across nodes; GPU and NIC on different CPU sockets; NCCL silently falling back to TCP sockets; ignoring link error counters until a job hangs.

Mental model: compute is rented by the hour, but you are often paying for GPUs that wait on the network.
subjects.project: Run all_reduce_perf on one node and across two nodes. Record busbw, compare with link specs, then deliberately break the IB binding (wrong NCCL_IB_HCA) and document how the logs and numbers change.

topics.title: Fabric Topology
topics.explainer: Topology decides achievable bandwidth. Read nvidia-smi topo -m: NV# means NVLink between GPUs, PIX/PXB means PCIe switches, SYS means crossing CPU sockets (slow). Each GPU should have a nearby NIC (rail-optimized designs pair GPU i on every node with the same switch rail). Know your numbers: NVLink on H100 is about 900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU, a 400 Gb/s NIC is 50 GB/s per direction, PCIe Gen5 x16 about 64 GB/s per direction. Plan placement so the heaviest traffic, usually tensor parallelism, stays on NVLink.

topics.title: NCCL Collectives
topics.explainer: NCCL chooses algorithm (ring, tree, NVLS) and transport (NVLink, IB verbs, sockets) per collective. Ring all-reduce sends 2(N-1)/N of the buffer per GPU; tree lowers latency for small messages; NVLink SHARP offloads reductions into NVSwitch. nccl-tests reports algbw and busbw: compare busbw with link speed to judge efficiency. Message size matters: small messages are latency-bound, large ones bandwidth-bound, so always sweep sizes. NCCL_DEBUG=INFO prints the chosen rings, channels and transports; that log is the first thing to read when performance looks wrong.

topics.title: Debugging Hangs & Slowdowns
topics.explainer: Slow or hung collectives usually come from one of a few causes: a straggler rank (bad GPU, thermal throttling, noisy neighbor), a degraded link (rising symbol errors or link flaps on IB ports), transport fallback to sockets, wrong interface selection, or ranks calling collectives in different orders. Tools: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS, ibstat and perfquery for port counters, DCGM for NVLink errors, PyTorch's NCCL timeouts and flight recorder to find which rank is behind. Bisect: single node first, then pairs of nodes, to isolate the bad component.

quiz.q: nccl-tests busbw far below link speed most likely indicates…
choices: A topology, transport or placement problem
quiz.why: busbw is normalized to compare with hardware link rates.

quiz.q: In nvidia-smi topo -m, 'SYS' between a GPU and NIC means…
choices: Traffic crosses the CPU interconnect between sockets
quiz.why: SYS paths are the slowest; pick a NIC on the GPU's socket.

quiz.q: Ring all-reduce traffic per GPU is approximately…
quiz.why: It stays near 2× buffer regardless of GPU count.

quiz.q: A good first step for a multi-node hang is…
choices: Find the lagging rank with timeouts/flight recorder and check that node's logs
quiz.why: Hangs usually trace to one rank or link.

subjects.title: GPU Sharing & Batch Scheduling on Kubernetes
subjects.why: GPUs are too expensive to leave idle or to hand out one whole card at a time.
subjects.explainer:
The GPU Operator turns Kubernetes nodes into GPU nodes: driver, container toolkit, device plugin, DCGM exporter, MIG manager and feature discovery. On top, you choose how to share: MIG for hard isolation, time-slicing for dev density, MPS for concurrent kernels. DRA gives pods richer device requests. Kueue and Volcano add the queueing, quotas, fair share and gang scheduling that batch and training jobs need.

Common mistakes: time-slicing production inference (no memory isolation); no quotas, so one team grabs every GPU; running distributed jobs without gang scheduling, causing partial-allocation deadlocks.

Goal: high utilization with predictable performance for the workloads that need it.
subjects.project: On a GPU node, install the GPU Operator, enable time-slicing with 4 replicas, then switch a second GPU to a MIG mixed profile. Run the same small model on both and compare latency under a noisy neighbor. Add Kueue with two team queues and show fair sharing.

topics.title: GPU Operator & Device Stack
topics.explainer: The GPU Operator manages the whole node-side stack as Kubernetes resources: driver containers (or pre-installed drivers), the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, the device plugin advertising nvidia.com/gpu, GPU Feature Discovery labels (model, memory, MIG capability), the DCGM exporter for metrics, and the MIG manager. Upgrades roll through nodes like any DaemonSet, which is why driver upgrades need maintenance windows and drains. Node labels from feature discovery let you schedule by GPU model or memory size instead of hard-coding node names.

topics.title: MIG, Time-Slicing & MPS
topics.explainer: MIG partitions supported GPUs (A100, H100, newer) into isolated instances with dedicated SMs and memory; profiles like 1g.10gb or 3g.40gb are fixed, and changing them requires the GPU to be idle. Time-slicing advertises a GPU as several replicas with no isolation, ideal for notebooks and CI. MPS lets processes run kernels concurrently with optional SM limits, improving throughput for many small inference workers. In the GPU Operator these are configured via ConfigMaps and node labels. Pick by isolation need: production multi-tenant means MIG; dev density means time-slicing.

topics.title: Dynamic Resource Allocation
topics.explainer: Device plugins only expose integer counts. DRA introduces DeviceClasses and ResourceClaims so a pod can ask for devices by attributes (GPU model, memory, MIG profile, interconnect) and share a claimed device between containers. Drivers publish ResourceSlices describing available devices; the scheduler matches claims against them, optionally with CEL selectors. DRA graduated to general availability in recent Kubernetes releases, and NVIDIA ships a DRA driver. Expect it to become the standard way to request accelerators, including multi-node NVLink domains.

topics.title: Kueue & Volcano
topics.explainer: Batch jobs need queues, not first-come scheduling. Kueue adds ClusterQueues with quotas per resource flavor (for example H100 versus L4), LocalQueues per team, borrowing of unused quota, preemption, and all-or-nothing admission for gang-style jobs. Volcano is a batch scheduler with gang scheduling, queues and fair share, popular for Spark, MPI and training. Both prevent the classic deadlock where two distributed jobs each hold half the GPUs they need. Pair them with PriorityClasses so production serving can preempt experiments.

choices: Allowing attribute-based device requests via ResourceClaims

subjects.why: Different dashboards than web CPUs.

DCGM, engine metrics, AI API SLIs, power/carbon. Runbooks for NCCL hangs, OOM, thrash, quality drops. Error budgets.

Quality is an SLI.

topics.title: Metrics
topics.explainer: DCGM exposes GPU metrics: SM activity, memory bandwidth, temperature, power, ECC and XID errors. Engine metrics (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM) cover queue depth, KV usage, TTFT and token rates. Add AI API SLIs per route. Track power and estimated carbon. Join metrics with cost so dashboards show dollars per million tokens, not just utilization. Try it: build one dashboard row that shows SM activity, HBM bandwidth, power, tokens per second and dollars per million tokens side by side.

topics.title: Operations
topics.explainer: Write runbooks for common incidents: GPU fell off the bus, NCCL hang, OOM loops, KV thrash, provider outage. Use error budgets to balance velocity and stability. Know the incident archetypes so on-call recognizes them quickly. Run blameless postmortems. Page on quality regressions as well as availability, since a model that answers wrongly at full speed is still an outage. Try it: pick the last three GPU incidents and check whether a runbook existed; write the missing ones while memory is fresh.

subjects.title: Infra Security & Isolation
subjects.why: Multi-tenant GPUs are hard.
subjects.explainer:
Namespaces, MIG, sandboxes, egress, signed images/SBOMs, model provenance, admission, secrets, confidential computing.

Common mistake: shared root-capable GPU containers. Another: unsigned model blobs.

Defense in depth.
subjects.project: Tenant isolation design: network policies, secrets, MIG vs nodes.

topics.title: Isolation
topics.explainer: Isolation for GPU workloads uses namespaces and network policies, MIG for hardware-partitioned GPUs, and sandbox runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers for untrusted code. Control egress tightly so a compromised workload cannot exfiltrate weights or data. Confidential computing on recent GPUs encrypts memory and attests the environment, protecting data even from the host operator. Rule of thumb: the more untrusted the code, the stronger the boundary: namespace, then gVisor, then microVM. Try it: run an agent's code tool in gVisor and test egress blocking.

topics.title: Supply Chain
topics.explainer: Sign container images and model artifacts, and keep SBOMs. Record model provenance: where weights came from and their hashes. Prefer safetensors over pickle-based formats, which can execute code on load. Admission controllers block unsigned or unscanned images. Store secrets in a vault, never in images or env files baked into models. Set SLAs for patching vulnerabilities. Try it: convert a pickle checkpoint to safetensors, sign it, and configure the loader to refuse unsigned or pickle files.

quiz.why: Stronger boundaries limit escape and exfiltration.

topics.explainer: Clouds offer managed model APIs, managed Kubernetes with GPU node pools, spot GPUs, marketplace models, and serverless GPU platforms that scale to zero. Managed services cut operational load; raw GPU instances give control and often better unit cost at scale. Most organizations use a mix. A good default: start on managed APIs to learn demand, then move steady high-volume traffic to self-hosted capacity once utilization data proves the savings. Try it: price one workload both ways.

topics.explainer: GPU quotas are scarce and approved per region, so request them well ahead. Use private networking to reach model endpoints without the public internet. Set up cross-account roles so teams share capacity safely. Alert on cost anomalies daily, since a forgotten 8-GPU node costs thousands per week. Build GPU workloads into your landing zone with guardrails from the start. Try it: set a daily budget alert per GPU project and a tag policy that blocks untagged GPU instances.

subjects.title: Energy, Power & Cooling
subjects.why: Watts are first-class constraints.
subjects.explainer:
Rack density, liquid cooling, PUE, carbon-aware shifting, utility lead times. Energy per 1M tokens as FinOps/ESG metric.

Common mistake: BOM facilities cannot power. Another: no summer thermal headroom.

topics.title: Facilities
topics.explainer: AI racks draw 40 to 130+ kW versus under 10 kW for classic servers. Air cooling tops out around 30 to 40 kW per rack; beyond that you need rear-door heat exchangers or direct liquid cooling. PUE (facility power divided by IT power) measures overhead. Utility power can take years to provision, which now gates AI expansion more than GPU supply. Plan redundancy for power and cooling, not just servers.

topics.title: Ops/ESG
topics.explainer: Measure energy per million tokens so efficiency improvements are visible. Carbon-aware scheduling moves flexible batch work to times or regions with cleaner power. Reporting rules increasingly require energy and emissions disclosure. Thermal incidents (cooling failures) can throttle or shut down racks within minutes, so monitor and alert on inlet temperatures. Efficiency gains from quantization and better batching directly cut power.

quiz.why: Facilities bound GPUs.

quiz.q: PUE is…
choices: Total facility power divided by IT power
quiz.why: A PUE of 1.2 means 20% overhead.

quiz.q: Air cooling generally stops being practical around…
quiz.why: Beyond that, liquid or rear-door cooling is needed.

subjects.title: GPU Failure Operations
subjects.why: At scale, GPUs fail weekly; the skill is turning failures into routine operations.
subjects.explainer:
Large clusters see constant hardware faults: memory ECC errors, GPUs falling off the bus, NVLink errors, overheating, and the hangs they cause in collective jobs. Good GPU operations read Xid codes, run DCGM diagnostics, drain and reset automatically, file RMAs with evidence, and keep training jobs resilient through checkpoints and spares.

Common mistakes: rescheduling jobs onto a node that just threw a fatal Xid; no health check between jobs; checkpoint intervals so long that each failure costs hours.

Half of AI SRE work lives here.
subjects.project: Write a node health controller: watch dmesg for Xids and DCGM health, classify them, cordon and drain on fatal codes, run dcgmi diag level 2 before returning the node, and open a ticket with logs on repeats. Test it with simulated log lines.

topics.title: Xid & ECC Errors
topics.explainer: Xid events are driver-reported faults in the kernel log. Some point at applications (13 graphics engine exception, 31 MMU fault), others at hardware: 48 double-bit ECC, 63/64 row remapping events, 74 NVLink error, 79 GPU fell off the bus, 92 high single-bit ECC rate, 94/95 contained and uncontained ECC errors on recent GPUs. Modern GPUs remap bad memory rows and need a reset to apply remaps; nvidia-smi -q shows remapped rows and pending remaps. Decide per class: investigate the app, reset, drain, or RMA.

topics.title: NCCL Hangs & Stragglers
topics.explainer: A collective waits for every rank, so one slow or dead GPU stalls thousands. Symptoms: step time spikes, all GPUs idle or spinning, no progress logs. Turn on NCCL and PyTorch timeouts so hangs become errors, enable the flight recorder to dump which collective each rank is in, and compare: the rank that is behind is the suspect. Check its node for Xids, thermal throttling or link errors. Stragglers that are slow but alive show up as consistent per-rank step time outliers; track them as a metric.

topics.title: Remediation Automation
topics.explainer: Manual triage does not scale past a few hundred GPUs. Automate a loop: detect (Xid watcher, DCGM health, failed jobs), classify, act (cordon, drain, GPU reset, node reboot), verify (DCGM diagnostics, a short burn-in or nccl-test), and return or escalate to RMA with logs attached. Keep spare nodes so jobs restart immediately. Measure mean time to detect and repair, and the share of GPU-hours lost to failures; that number justifies investment in checkpoints and spares.
